utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Could we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 13th of July, 2005, I'd like to greet everyone present, the three representatives of the Prosecution, the five Defence lawyers, as well as General Hadzihasanovic and Brigadier Kubura. I would also like to greet everyone else in the courtroom. Today the Prosecution will be completing its closing argument, after which General Hadzihasanovic's Defence shall commence with its closing argument. As far as I have been told, the Prosecution has another two hours and 42 minutes available. I don't know how many seconds they have remaining. Without wasting any more time, I will now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. And to my colleagues, good morning. Mr. President, yesterday at the end of the session I delivered my submission with respect to Bugojno in a very condensed form because of the constraints of time. But nevertheless, even though it was condensed, I think it was sufficient enough to convey the Prosecution's point with respect to the facilities in Bugojno. One striking thing about the facilities in Bugojno is that it is common to all the other facilities -- all the other detention facilities that were operated by the ABiH 3rd Corps and also all the facilities, including those in Bugojno, had within it two common threats: One, the physical conditions -- the deplorable physical conditions that existed in the facilities; and, two, the cruel and inhumane treatment that all detainees were subjected to endure. And I think even though I may have raced it through, I think the Trial Chamber would have been appraised of -- of the situation at the time in Bugojno in the detention facilities. As I indicated as well yesterday afternoon, that the second limb of my submission deals with the notice aspect with respect to the accused General Hadzihasanovic and the Bugojno facilities. Mr. President, Your Honours, I wish to submit, or I believe that there can be no doubt -- or rather, there should be no doubt in the minds of Your Lordships that the evidence presented by the Prosecution in the conduct of this case through its witnesses and its -- in its final brief and in the conduct of -- and again here today and yesterday has demonstrated that the soldiers of the ABiH 3rd Corps, in particular the soldiers and military police of the OG Zapad and the 307th Motorised Brigade, operated a number of detention facilities in its -- in its AOR, including those located in the town of Bugojno. Further, contrary to the submissions in the final brief for the Defence of the accused General Hadzihasanovic, there is no doubt that each and every one of these facilities run by the ABiH soldiers of the 3rd Corps subordinated to the accused General Hadzihasanovic mistreated, surrendered, and captured HVO soldiers and Bosnian civilians alike. Similarly, that these detention facilities, and in particular Bugojno of which I now address you, were at all times guarded by soldiers of the ABiH 3rd Corps. And even more, there is absolutely no doubt that the evidence produced demonstrated at all times the accused General Hadzihasanovic was aware that these ABiH soldiers under his command committed the crimes as it relates to -- as it relates to Bugojno, as alleged in the indictment before Your Honours today. Your Honours, much has been said and has been made by the Defence in their final closing brief as to whether the accused General Hadzihasanovic possessed the required notice in respect of Bugojno so as to satisfy the requirements under the -- the Statute. Your Honours, in this light, there is much evidence to support the Prosecution's allegations, and I wish to draw your attention, Your Honour, first to footnote 1005, page 169 of the Prosecution's final brief. In the interests of time, I would not be able to read out the entire note, but from the evidence led one sees that as early as the 24th of July, 1993, the accused Hadzihasanovic was aware that his subordinates had captured a large number of soldiers, of HVO soldiers, and detained an even larger number -- and detained an even larger number of non-Bosniak civilians, and in this regard, Your Honour, I would like Your Honours during your deliberations to consider Prosecution's 437 -- P437, and P608. Again, on the 26th of July, 1993 there's the order from Senad Dautovic [phoen], Prosecution Exhibit P654, and again the order of Rasim Delic of the 27th of July, 1993, when he wrote to the 3rd Corps Command expressing his concern about the treatment of the Croatian population in Bugojno and ordering that the HVO members who participated in combat against the unit should be treated as prisoners of war and they should act towards them in accordance with provisions of the Geneva Conventions on prisoners of war. Despite the above, the evidence reveals that the accused Hadzihasanovic failed to take the requisite steps to act. For example, Your Honours, he failed to implement the said order of Rasim Delic on the 27th of July, 1993, immediately or even to merely ascertain whether the foundations of the numerous -- to ascertain the foundations of the numerous allegations. Aside from that, the Prosecution has fielded witnesses, the famous (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I could go on and on, Your Honour, but time does not permit and I ask Your Honours or I draw Your Honours' attention to Prosecution Exhibit 441. This in a synopsis shows that only some several weeks later, on the 14th of September, 1993, did -- the accused Hadzihasanovic instructed the commands of OG --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 441 in a synopsis shows that only some several weeks later, on the 14th of September, 1993, did the accused General Hadzihasanovic instruct the commander of OG Zapad 307th Motorised Brigade to provide the International Red Cross with access to HVO POWs in Bugojno on the 20th and 21st of September, 1993. Of note, some three or four months later after the said report, alerting him of the tortures, cruel treatment, and deaths. Your Honour, then we see that the -- the access to the ECMM and to the locals, the accused failed to -- to allow any access -- or rather, through his subordinates only much later and step by step, contrary to the spirit of the Geneva Conventions. The allegations of the deaths of Mario Zrno and Mladen Havranek, who had been beaten black and blue and resulting in their untimely deaths and for which the authorities after investigation found out that the allegations were in fact through -- were in fact well-founded and true, is indeed another instance of where General Hadzihasanovic was in fact very well made aware of what transpired and what was going on in the detention centres of Bugojno. Another witness testified that upon his return from visiting Bugojno he personally wrote a report about the reported incident in the furniture salon, in which a prisoner detainee had died. He further stated that he forwarded the report to his superior. These are just but a few instances in the evidence that was led with respect to the notice that the Prosecution says that was implied to General Hadzihasanovic. These are a few -- the few instances on which General Hadzihasanovic was very much aware or made aware of what was -- what transpired in the detention centres of Bugojno and for which he failed to -- to take any action either to prevent or to punish the alleged perpetrators. Mr. President and Your Honours, in the Prosecution's -- in the Prosecution's humble view, this fully satisfies the -- under the law and demonstrates that the accused General Hadzihasanovic did in fact have sufficient notice to initiate investigations of which he failed to carry out, and if he indeed did so and did so -- and if he indeed did so, did so when it was a little too late in the day, long after the alleged breaches were committed. Unless Your Honours need any further assistance by way of clarifications, Your Lordships, this, in my humble submission, on behalf of the Prosecution, is the position as it relates to counts 3 and 4 of Bugojno, the town of Bugojno in the municipality of Bugojno. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. In a few seconds, I will start with presentation on Guca Gora in June 1993, followed by Orasac in October 1993, and by Vares in November 1993, so I try to follow a chronological order. First of all, Guca Gora -- or ABiH control over Guca Gora was established on the 8th of June, 1993. P465, a regular operations report from the OG Bosanska Krajina, which has the time code 1900 hours in its letterhead, says: "The 306th Mountain Brigade captured the village of Guca Gora." The question is whether there was any prevention, especially on that morning of the 8th of June in Travnik, a few kilometres away. There was an incident with Mujahedins who had entered and demolished a charge, St. John the Baptist in Travnik, and at the time the ABiH had established control over Guca Gora in the course of the day. This incident must have been known since Witness Cuskic had been early in the morning already in Travnik and had seen what had been done there to the church. I want to talk briefly about the status of Guca Gora village at the period of the ABiH takeover and Witness Camdzic told Your Honours: "As we were walking through Guca Gora, I couldn't see any damages. There may have been some burnt-down stables and cowsheds, but the rest of the village was intact. There was no -- there were no damages." What has been observed by other witnesses was that furniture was standing particularly outside the monastery or on the street; for example, on the 13th of June, one witness, Bower said, "There was a lot of furniture outside the church." Similarly, on the 16th of June, Witness Mahir testified, "There were some objects in front of the monastery." And again, another witness on the 12th of June, Mr. Radic, through his binoculars from Cifluk, a nearby villager, he observed, "The tractors and the trailers would be parked before our convent in Guca Gora," and he saw people in uniform and he saw also civilians, the women wearing baggy Muslim trousers. So the Prosecution submits that there's an indication that the surrounding of the monastery where the furniture was seen, that this furniture might indicate that there was a collection point around the monastery. I want to deal now with the Mujahedin and especially the difficult question: How did the Mujahedin come to Guca Gora? First of all, the exact time of the Mujahedins' arrival to Guca Gora is unclear; however, there is certain indications about their movements before, in the days before. The first document I want to show to Your Honours is dating on the 22nd of May, and you see here the excerpt from Semir Terzic, and -- this is P474, and you see in Mehurici at the time, 22nd May, 1993, you have 92 soldiers from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. On the 25th of May -- this is DH1071, a official note from Witness Delalic to the military security of the 3rd Corps. He mentions a group of Mujahedin billeted in Mehurici, and they reconnoitered an elevation: Probijeno Brdo, elevation 1009. If Your Honours would look at the following map, you see this elevation, 1009, and you see the name, Probijeno Brdo. So on the 25th of May, 1993, you see the movements of the Mujahedin. And if I go back, it says: "The group of Mujahedin was led by Ramo Durmis." On the 27th of May, there's a transfer order from Mehurici to Radojcici, that's P481, and it says in the relevant part: "The commander of the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade redeployed 20 soldiers from Mehurici sector to Radojcici village." Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that this commander of the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion was indeed Ramo Durmis. If Your Honours have a moment and look at the map here, you see that Radojcici is in the lower part, about one and a half, two, up to three kilometres away from Guca Gora, and this transfer was on the 27th. The question is: Was it carried out? On 29th of May, 1993, there was reconnaissance around Radojcici, and you see here a report from a war diary of the 306th Mountain Brigade, C18, and it's -- the relevant excerpt says: "At 1300 hours, during the daylight, report from Radojcici that a scout missing of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade." So this indicates the transfer had indeed taken place. What was the objective of the reconnaissance? Your Honours, you have been in Guca Gora, and I was informed you have been also in Cifluk. I want to show Your Honours for a -- a little excerpt from a videotape now. And since you have been already on -- on site, I want to ask you to try to remember where the towers of the church, the front of the church, in which direction was the front of the church located, so to speak, inside the valley. And I'm showing Your Honours a little portion here from 1 hours, 8 minutes, 34 seconds onwards on P482.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours have just seen this little excerpt, and you have seen where the towers were standing, and I'm asking Your Honours for one moment simply to look again at the map. The monastery is encircled here. Just for a moment to look at the map and see from which angle this reconnaissance of the monastery was carried out. Your Honours have seen the video in the course of this trial. You know the following story, that a certain group is then moving into the monastery. I want to talk about the strength of the Mujahedin at the monastery. Merdan visits around 11th and 12th of June, 1993. He's there for four to five hours. And how many Mujahedin does he see? "Ten to fifteen were in the courtyard, mostly foreigners, and at least a translator," that's what he says. At the arrest operation a couple of days later, the senior commander Mahir describes the group. He mentions several foreigners, Arabs, and then he also mentions local people, "maybe 15 or 20 among those we saw." So then he goes on and says, "The total number, not more than 25. 20 to 25." So it looks like the group was almost stable between 15, 10 to 20, 25 men. Two days after the -- or a few days after the visits of Merdan, Hadzihasanovic writes to the Supreme Command, "I am requesting your stances and opinions regarding the solution to this problem." Your Honours have heard evidence on how finally the Mujahedin or, let's say, the military police was facing the Mujahedin. The question is: When were the military police men tasked by the 3rd Corps? And Witness Mahir says, "On the 15th or 16th of June." He isn't quite sure about this. So between the time, let's say, the Mujahedin had moved in, Merdan had met them around 11th or 12th, and the 15th and 16th, when the task was issued, there was time to prepare. The Mujahedin had stayed already for days around the monastery. And as I said, there was a clearly reduced mobility. The group was -- the size of the group was sort of stable. And unlike the locations in Mehurici and Orasac from this group, the monastery -- which were in a distant valley -- the monastery itself is lying at a main road, between the two main cities, Travnik and Zenica. So reinforcement for an operation was easily -- was easily possible to get, especially since the territory had been freshly liberated. What was the mandate of the operation finally, the military police operation? Mr. Mahir testified, "It was our aim to enter the facility and protect it from being destroyed. That was our main goal. We wanted to fulfil the assignment we had been given in Zenica to protect." So just -- there was no rest mandate, it looks like. What are the resources provided by the 3rd Corps for this task? Mr. Mahir testified, "There was a total of 26 of us, 13 -- excuse me, 16 3rd Corps military police and then 10 -- about 10 soldiers from the 306th Brigade." So during the time the military police was on the spot, Mr. Mahir said, "We even threatened to bring in reinforcements from Zenica, that another unit would come to assist us." However, Mahir indicated, "We didn't have any touch unit," so obviously the resources provided by the corps weren't that extensive. Then Mr. Mahir goes on: "I wouldn't try to arrest anyone. I wouldn't protect the facility I was sent to protect. There are other people who will arrest, establish the identity, and do all those other things." He even talks about an agreement. If I can use a civilian expression, "We reached an agreement and then we entered the premises. And that was our goal. It wasn't our intention to arrest anybody." In which direction did the Mujahedin leave, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MAHIR ANSWERS THAT
utterances.text: "They went towards Travnik, towards the village. We didn't follow them." He says later: "I would say they went off to the area controlled by the 3rd Corps." Witness HF -- Witness HE - excuse me - Witness Sefer and Eminovic were all working in the security sector or in the exchange sector, so they took statements. So they were familiar with investigative techniques. They arrived after the monastery had been secured; however, they took no pictures of the Arabic inscriptions. What did they do? They painted them over. They took no statements, no documentation of the damage. It had been claimed that the 306 military police had been there in Guca Gora. Why weren't the 306 Military Police -- in the days before the securing of the monastery, why weren't the military police of the 306th Brigade not interviewed? In effect, the painting-over of the inscriptions without taking pictures means an alteration of a fresh crime site. Your Honours, I want to address the question: Was the SVK, the Supreme Command, in favour of the agreement option that the Mujahedin could leave? There is an order from Delic, the supreme commander, on the 16th of June to Hadzihasanovic, and it's straightforward and says: "Send these groups to Igman ... in case they do not accept it, show them no hospitality and eventually disarm them." Your Honours will note that this order -- it states at the very end of this order it was sent at 1515 hours on the 16th of June, and I mentioned earlier Mahir isn't quite sure when he had received his task with the military police, on the 15th or on the 16th. So it is not exactly clear whether this order relates to Guca Gora, comes shortly thereafter, whether there were any discussions between the Supreme Command and the 3rd Corps before. This order was sent 1515 hours on the 16th. And following that -- or on the same day, there is a conversation, a telephone conversation between Hadzihasanovic and Halilovic. This is DH165-3. The exact event and the topic of the conversation is not really clear. The Prosecution noted Visoko and not Guca Gora is several times mentioned, so it is not entirely clear what the main topic of that conversation is. However, I want to read out a small excerpt from it. "D," standing for Dzedo [phoen] and "S," standing for Sefer. This is a submission from the Prosecution. "Regarding the information that we have received," Dzedo says, "about those foreigners, yes, it cannot be done that way. "Really?" "No way. It is my third front line." Sefer: "No, no, but try. It is ordered, here, two of them have signed it, go. Do you understand me?" Dzemo [phoen] says: "Try to send an order without that second part, ordering only to send them up there." Your Honours can see at the very beginning Dzemo mentions information he has received. What information had Hadzihasanovic available on the 16th of June, 1993? I have mentioned already there was a five -- four- to five-hour long encounter with the Mujahedin already by 10th of June in Merdan, and he says, "I reported to Hadzihasanovic." And Witness HF has testified to Your Honours, when asked about Ramo Durmis - I quote - "There were reports saying that he was with a small group around the monastery of Guca Gora, a group of Mujahedin causing problems there, when the army wanted to protect the monastery." End of quote. So a small group; this is what Witness HF has mentioned. Again, it is not entirely clear, since Visoko is mentioned in the conversation I cited earlier, to which event this conversation relates to but it certainly relates to foreigners and the dealing with these problems. Witness Duncan commented on Delic's order, and he says: " ... Having been given this order, Hadzihasanovic has to then make a decision as to where his priorities lie." Your Honours, it's the Prosecution's submission the manpower provided for the Guca Gora securing operation indicates the commander's priorities. I'm not exactly sure about the precise figure, but the corps had roughly about 25.000, 27.000 men at its disposal. A cease-fire with the HVO was concluded on the 13th of June, 1993. It's DH238, so at around the time of the Guca Gora securing, the cease-fire was in effect. And how many soldiers or military policemen were sent? Twenty-six. The question is: How big was the threat posed by the Mujahedin in Guca Gora really and how big was this threat in the eyes of the 3rd Corps officers? There is an indication from Merdan's visit around the 11th and 12th of June. The question is: Was Merdan on that visit accompanied by several soldiers to ensure his security? I will quote from the cross-examination of Mr. Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "You told us you were with your driver on that occasion. Is that correct? Your driver drove you there?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MERDAN
utterances.text: "Yes, the driver was by the vehicle. And only the driver witnessed that scene, yes." Kent-Payne told Your Honours an analysis he had heard from Mr. Merdan at the 3rd Corps headquarters on the 30th of June, 1993. He said, and I quote, an analogy on the lines of: "But you have to understand that, that the foreigners are like the -- the genie in Aladdin, then. You can rub the lamp and get the genie out to help you. But unlike the genie who returns to the lamp, then the foreigners are very difficult to get back into their box and they're difficult to control." Merdan's explanation: "I'm not familiar with the symbolism of Aladdin's lamp. Perhaps I wanted to say that the issues of the foreigners was a complex issue, if they were there, and we had information according to which they were present in June 1993." I want to move a little bit away from the securing of the monastery and look just at the agreement option, which was finally adopted because it was obviously favoured by the 3rd Corps. Again, the agreement option marks a lost opportunity to discipline the Mujahedin unit. All individual perpetrators as a result, since they could leave Guca Gora, the whole unit and all individual perpetrators remained in the territory of the 3rd Corps AOR. So if you don't get rid of these people, they're remaining in your AOR. So retrospectively, the Guca Gora-securing operation is important; it marks a crucial event, because if I don't expel these people, as I'm ordered - whether later or not - if I don't expel these people, they're staying on my territory. So basically retrospectively this is preceding the formation of the El Mujahedin Battalion. If I don't get rid of these people, they're staying with me, I basically give them the status, which happened eight weeks later, of a unit, of a detachment. Having said this, I want to move to Orasac, an event after the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment. First of all, the foreseeable conduct of the abductions. When soldiers of the Mujahedin were captured by the HVO, that unit responded with own abductions of Croats. So these are the lessons learned from the Totic abduction, which was just a couple of months before the events unfolding in Orasac. It says: "On the 3rd of October, C13, war diary of the OG Bosanska Krajina at 0800 hours, five Mujahedin soldiers crossed over to the Ustasha zone by car. The outcome is unknown." A more detailed description is given by Witness HE. He says: "Towards the end of September 1993, a group of five Mujahedin lost their way as they were travelling from Opara, following a UNHCR convoy. As the convoy was passing all the checkpoints, they reached the village of Trenica. The convoy passed, the Mujahedin followed them, and they entered Novi Travnik. And the four of them were killed there on the spot; the fifth one, who was the interpreter, I suppose, he was a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina ... I learned that from Abu Dzafer." Your Honours, mentioned are Opara and Trenica. Just to mention on the map where that is, Opara is south of Novi Travnik, as is Trenica, as Your Honours can see. This will be reviewed in a moment. The survivor, the interpreter, as Witness HE said, says: "The unit was stationed in Mehurici and from there we were sent to the front lines." And he goes on: "After the failed attack, we were supposed to return to Novi Travnik." And later on he mentions the people who were killed, and he mentions Vahidin. Your Honours have heard the name of Valjudin [phoen] several times during that trial. The Prosecution submits Vahidin or Valjudin is one and the same person, the military commander of that unit at that time. Abu Dzafer visits Witness HE on a daily basis this. This has been put on the record, and he even said to Witness HE he would pick up as many Croats as necessary. Then on the 7th of October -- this is P709 -- on the 7th of October, 1993, Beba makes an announcement at an exchange commission meeting with the HVO, "Unless Kadiric was released from Croat detention - and here's the quote - "20 innocent Croats would be arrested in Travnik every day, Croats who had voluntarily opted to stay under BH army control." End of quote. Your Honours have heard evidence about the two abduction waves, the first one about a week after that comment and the second one 18th and 19th of October, ten days roughly after this comment. Your Honours have heard evidence that civilians were abducted in both abduction waves; clerics in the first, and I have listed here the other civilians from the -- from the second abduction wave. One person was even 17 years old. They were brought to Orasac. Your Honours have heard evidence about this. This was not a secret location. Rather, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had meetings there, as early as July and August 1993. The Prosecution's referring to P501, P500, P611. Just P611 dating 10th of August, days before the formation of the El Mujahedin Unit. The relevant part reads: "The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade forward command post remains in Orasac village and there are no plans for it to be relocated." And, Your Honours, this is sent to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade commander, a forward command post in Orasac village. What is the knowledge of the ABiH officers about the abduction? It was notorious. Ms. Popovic conducted -- contacted many, many authorities, Mr. Cuskic, Mr. Alagic, civilian military authorities alike. On the 18th of October, you have a conversation between Duncan and Hadzihasanovic. On P216 it is noted. Here is the document. And the relevant part reads: "Questions on the actions of the Muslim extremists towards remaining Croat minorities in BiH-controlled areas. Hadzihasanovic side-stepped the issue completely. He did not acknowledge that there was a problem." This is on the 15th, the first abduction wave; on the 18th/19th, the second abduction wave starts. And, Your Honours, this is on the 18th of October. And, again, Witness HE, before the second abduction wave, what is he -- what has he testified to Your Honours? "Abu Haris lied to me several hours prior to the kidnapping when he told me that no further measures would have been taken." So there is contact. Your Honours, I want to draw your attention to the 22nd of October, 1993. Mr. Duncan spoke to Mr. Merdan, source P226. Here is the document. The relevant part reads: "Mr. Merdan stated that the 3rd Corps had tasked Mr. Alagic, commander of the OG Bosanska Krajina, to resolve the ongoing problem with the Mujahedin in Travnik." Duncan, when questioned on P226 stated - and this is a question by Mr. Bourgon - "Would you agree with me that this specific -- what Mr. Merdan was referring to at that time had nothing to do with what we are talking about now of resubordination but actually dealt with five Croats which had been kidnapped by unknown Mujahedin elements in Travnik? Would that recall some souvenirs for you?" Mr. Duncan says: "Yes." So they talked about, according to Duncan's recollection, the abductions, again, on the 22nd of October. Merdan, when questioned by Judge Swart on that same document said: "I can claim with full responsibility that Duncan Alastair never told me that some Croats had been kidnapped in Travnik." The opposite. So what is the correct interpretation, Your Honours, of P226, referring to this remark from Mr. Merdan? Again, I want to point out Mr. Merdan's testimony. He says: "I signed an order or perhaps even two orders on behalf of the 3rd Corps commander according to which the El Mujahedin Detachment was to be resubordinated to the OG Bosanska Krajina, which was led by the late General Alagic. So if I said that, Colonel Alastair Duncan probably paraphrased what I said. But I would like to emphasise the fact that Duncan never told me that Croats had been kidnapped in Travnik." Mr. Merdan mentioned resubordination orders signed on behalf of the 3rd Corps commander. Was the resubordination during the Orasac Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. abductions? What does the war diary of the OG Bosanska Krajina tell Your Honours? On the 27th of October, an entry at 1900 hours - that's C13 - information about the 308th Brigades relating to the 24th of October, 1993. On that day, an attack was carried out on the HVO positions in the area of Novi Travnik, and there are villages mentioned, Rankovska Kosa, Rastovci, Zubicki. The attack started at 8.30. The commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment was wounded," the OG Bosanska Krajina reports. "We have four dead, 17 wounded soldiers. El Mujahedin has three dead and eight wounded." This indicates joint combat. Here are the locations just talked about, Zubicki, Rastovci, Rankovska Kosa. Your Honours will recall that the -- at the end of September, beginning of October, the killed El Mujahedins, Valjudin and so on, this was near Trenica, which was a little bit north of Rastovci, as Your Honours can see. And I will come to Rastovci in a moment. There is the arrest of 7th Krajina Mountain Brigade soldier Kuduzovic one day after this joint combat, and Cuskic has testified to Your Honours: "The delegation arrived at my barracks, asked to be received by me. We spent more than two hours in difficult discussions, and this resulted in them apologising and releasing this soldier." He was asked: "Who was part of that delegation?" And Mr. Cuskic says - I just quote - "On behalf of the Mujahedin, Abu Haris, the Emir, the commander of that unit." Again the war diary of the OG Bosanska Krajina, 27th of October, 1235 hours, reporting. Basically the Mujahedin requested a signature of one of his commanders for the release from Novi Travnik. And who was getting it from Novi Travnik? Your Honours have just seen the map. Beba took measures to get it. The release is occurring on the 27th of October, and there is a mentioning in that war diary - it's P711 or C13, 27th of October - Beba is again mentioned. On that day there was a conversation again, Beba with ECMM, about Alagic, what is he saying, and the Mujahedin: "Presently, Alagic has other concerns. When these are over, he will demand control." DH1968, paragraph 7. Two days later, on the 29th of October -- excuse me, on the 27th of October, after the release, Alagic makes a statement to the ECMM. As for hostages are civilians didn't so he's not talking about Kuduzovic; he's talking about the hostages for whom the Prosecution has launched this section of the indictment. "As the hostages are civilians, strictly speaking the matter was outside his control." And he added -- listen, Your Honours. What is Mr. Alagic saying? "He is due to meet the Mujahedin tonight." P177, paragraph 5. And this same meeting you find another important entry on P178, another detail. In this conversation, it was discussed: "There are shots at a convoy near -- on a convoy near Novi Travnik, and the location is Rastovci." Your Honours have heard about it. And in that conversation on the 27th or 29th - I'm not sure at the moment - of October, what is Mr. Alagic saying? And I have displayed that for Your Honours. He says: "Alagic denied that his troops had been in that area" -- and I'm referring to Rastovci here -- "but he suggested that Mujahedin units could have been there and he would not know" -- listen -- "because they reported directly to the 3rd Corps BiH." And he's talking about Rastovci area. Where is Rastovci? Your Honours, if you look for a moment on this map, you see it's again near Novi Travnik. There is continuing notice of the 3rd Corps about combat, joint combat in that area. So the question is, Mr. Alagic has said, they reported directly to the 3rd Corps. So in October 1993, to whom did the Mujahedin report to, as Alagic, who must know it, suggests. And an answer is partially provided in P618. It's an extraordinary report sent to the command of the 3rd Corps. And, Your Honours, "Attention the commander." Why? It's from the 9th of October, so six days prior to the first abduction wave from Orasac. "Representatives of the detachment El Mujahedin visited me today," Mr. Cikotic writes, "and they stated their readiness to engage a part of the their unit in activities in the area of Gornji Vakuf." Not Novi Travnik this time; it's Gornji Vakuf, Your Honours. "According to them, it is conditioned with your orders. It is a list." Did they report to Enver Hadzihasanovic? Again, I want to return to P226 and Merdan's comment. "I claim with full responsibility that I signed an order, or perhaps even two orders, on behalf of the 3rd Corps commander according to which the El Mujahedin Detachment was to be resubordinated ..." On the 3rd of November, you have a conversation with Sir Martin Garrod. When asked about the Mujahedin, Hadzihasanovic said, "there were several kinds," he says. And I quote just one sentence: "There was no special organisation of Mujahedin," Mr. Hadzihasanovic says. P181, page 8, paragraph 10. At the time Mr. Hadzihasanovic has made that comment, three civilians were still held in Orasac. I'm referring here to Ivo Fisic, Mr. Rajkovic, and Mr. Adzaip. They were released, Fisic and Rajkovic, 6 November, three days after that comment, and Mr. Adzaip, after the 5th, before the 11th of December, 1993. It's not exactly clear. So shortly before the release of Mr. Adzaip, as I said, around the 5th -- between the 5th and the 11th of December, there is an order of the 3rd Corps command, C13, 5 of December, 1530 hours. What does it say? "The El Mujahed Detachment is to be resubordinated to the OG." It is not "subordinated," Your Honours; it is "resubordinated." The question is: The Orasac abductions, were there measures taken, preventive measures. Beba -- Salko Beba had heard. He was -- about Abu Dzafer's intentions. He was in repeated daily contact with him. Repressive measures. I want to point Your Honours' attention to the Kuduzovic incident. The soldier from the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade. And here Your Honours see how repressive measures could work. Even a simple brigade, not a corps, a simple brigade, the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade, Mr. Cuskic could quickly -- or let's not say quickly -- but could get Mr. Kuduzovic released, and it didn't intention the intervention of the corps. It was Mr. Cuskic who threatened to mortar them. So there was some force or at least threat of force necessary. However, a simple brigade could reach the delegation that was visiting him. Abu Haris visited him after the threat. He took it serious. And my last point on Orasac is: Your Honours, please compare this incident with the Totic abduction and the measures, in quotation marks, the "measures" employed there. Were there investigations of the 3rd Corps military police? During Totic abduction, Your Honours have heard evidence. Were there measures from the 3rd Corps military police in Orasac taken? Was there any evidence led on ABiH cooperation with the CSB Zenica, like during the Totic abduction? Were there on-site visits to the known camps or locations of the Mujahedin? There were visits by Salko Beba, but were there on-site visits? And similarly, the comparison to the Totic abduction shows there were no visits by the HVO or international representatives to possible detention locations. There was no campaign to show basically the sites or the areas. There was no such campaign. Your Honours, I'm coming to my last topic, Vares. First of all, it overlaps to a certain degree from a timely perspective with Orasac. As I said earlier, Orasac goes on until the 5th of December. But the parallels end here. It is a separate incident. And Your Honours have heard evidence about the acts of anger and revenge by the ABiH forces who moved into an abandoned town. The question is: Were these acts of revenge and anger foreseeable? There was a Stupni Do massacre - Your Honours have heard evidence on this - in late October 1993. So this was a clear, clear signal that acts of revenge may occur, because this was a very, very serious crime committed by the HVO. And Mr. Hadzihasanovic in a conversation with Mr. Garrod - I'm referring to P181, page 7, paragraph 2 this time - he stated that: "Hadzihasanovic said he had just been to Vares. He said that the HVO had made a serious mistake and when there was a massacre, it was difficult to control their BiH soldiers." End of quote. This was in autumn 1993. And Witness Junuzevic have testified to Your Honours: "That period of time is well known for being a period of famine in Central Bosnia." And he goes on, "especially in Breza, Zenica, and Vares." There is a combat order sent by Mr. Hadzihasanovic to Kubura on the 3rd of November, 1993, and I'm referring to P674, paragraph 5. And you see the 3rd Corps commander is aware about that danger, or at that time actually formally Mr. Hadzihasanovic was no longer the 3rd Corps commander but this order is sent to Mr. Kubura. And it states, advising -- instructing Mr. Kubura: "Do not allow any revenge or massacres. Deal with war booty in the spirit of the 3rd Corps Command order." It was a multi-corps operation which unfolded to take Vares. Delic had tasked - it's DH1513 - three different corps, 2nd, 3rd, and 6th Corps. And within these corps, there was an OG East, and this reported to the 3rd Corps. And the order of Hadzihasanovic to Kubura on the 3rd of November in paragraph 4 - I mentioned it earlier, P674 - gives guidance who -- to whom Mr. Kubura has to report to. "The commander OG East shall command all forces to Vares." And Your Honours see in evidence certain orders from OG East reports back to the 3rd Corps. I'm referring to P445, P676, P793. In one instance - it's P446 - the 3rd Corps instructs the OG East, so it is clear who is reporting to whom. Mr. Kubura, the latest time he arrived at the forward command post in Strijezevo was on the 3rd of November. P46H -- 68, page 1. The question is: Was there a change in plans. Two documents, P674, paragraph 1, and P474 tell Your Honours about the axis which has been to be -- or on which the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had to operate. And initially the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was supposed to stay on these certain axes around Vares. However, P448, page 11 tells Your Honour also about one of these axes. The plan was to engage only the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade on the Visnjevik-Mir-Stupni Do-Tisovci-Przic-Dastansko axis Visnje cri-Mir-Stupni Do-Tisovci-Przic-Dastansko axis, and two [unintelligible]. However, source P468, page 1, tells Your Honours: "Our units arrived early in the morning of 3 November 1993, and during the night" - referring probably to the night 3 to 4 November - "We received a task from the brigade commander to go to Vares itself in the early hours of 4 November 1993." Stay on the axis or go to Vares itself. How did the -- in the multiple-corps operation, how did the other commanders or even superiors react to that change? And I'm referring here to the commander of the Vares tactical group and the Chief of Staff of OG East -- the superior to Amir Kubura. It's P448, page 11. What does the commander say? "The task was not carried out completely, because the troops did not get beyond Bijelo Borje and Tisovci but headed for the town instead." They were not staying on the axis; they headed for the town instead. And, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade spearheaded that southern operation to take Vares. Witness Podzic has told Your Honours: "About a quarter of an hour after we entered" -- meaning the outskirts of Vares. "About a quarter of an hour after we entered, several other units showed up." And what was the task of these units? "Their task" -- I quote. "Their task was to take over the lines that we had established." End of quote. Who had established these lines, Your Honours? The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade spearheading that operation from the south. Again P445, the commander of the 6th Corps mentions at a certain point in time, 1045 hours on the 4th of November, 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had entered Vares. And what is the result of this, Your Honours? "They are stealing and looting everything they see," P445 reports. And it is important that -- to whom does this "they" relate? If you follow the text here, the Chief of Staff of the Istok OG reported that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade -- or a battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had entered Vares by the main road." And here it comes: "They are stealing." There is no other unit mentioned here. It is the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade Battalion, and they are stealing and looting everything they see. Going again to the word everything. This word "everything" is also mentioned in P676. And it indicates the scale of destruction and looting. "This morning the ArBiH units (7th Muslim Mountain Brigade), entered the town of Vares. Their arrival in town created general chaos. Everything is being looted and burned." And then it comes: "Other combatants joined the looting and burning." And the question was: When was the joining? An insider of -- from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade is also reporting about war booty. He's in the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Your Honours have heard evidence this battalion was moving through Vares, was not staying in Majdan, was moving through Vares. And here Mr. Disdarevic [phoen], it is P468, page 2, mentions: "Battalion organisation of gathering war booty, primarily foodstuff, was done well, which could not be said of other brigade units or the brigade itself." Your Honours, an insider is reporting here about the gathering of war booty, primarily foodstuff. It was done well by his 2nd Battalion. But he goes on: "It could not be said the same -- it could not be said of other brigade units." He's not talking about other brigades; he's talking, the Prosecution submit, about his own brigade, "or the brigade itself." So there is obviously some organisation of the items which are taken in Vares. I want to turn to one aspect of destruction now, the cross-shooting in an abandoned town. First of all, the combat order from Mr. Hadzihasanovic mentioned already, P674, in paragraph 4 mentions: "If the town has been abandoned, organise an attack and liberate Vares." He's talking about an abandoned town. This is on the 3rd of November. Kubura reports or responds back in the night of the 3 to 4 November: "The population is fleeing in large numbers by passenger and freight vehicles." This must be the Croat population in Vares. And he continues: "The lower part of the town is completely empty." There were indication s the town was abandoned. So Kubura had reconnaissance available prior to the 7th descending to Vares that troops -- or that the town had been abandoned, especially the southern part. So then there was the cross-shooting occurring. And the Prosecution just wants to point out two points about it. Podzic had testified to Your Honours: "It was occurring at the outskirts of the city. Such a formation" - the V-formation; Your Honours have heard about it - "and such a movement was maintained until we entered the city." So it was only on the outskirts, Mr. Podzic has told Your Honours. Birger has told another story. He says: "We meet these attacking soldiers in the square, where the mayor's house is." Your Honours, where is the mayor's house in Vares? Where is the mayor's house? It is usually in the city centre. And Birger says so later on in his testimony: "I meet them in the middle of Vares, in the middle of Vares more or less. That means the square about the mayor's house." So was it at the outskirts or was it in the middle of Vares? Was the cross-shooting in V-formation only occurring at the outskirts or was it going on into the city senor? Who tells the truth? The Prosecution submits Birger was an independent observer, not part of the hostilities, and unlike Podzic Birger knew Vares pretty well. He was permanently stationed there at the time. So Mr. Birger and his orientation of Vares should be a good one. Kubura was in command and control during the operation. The order from 1st of November, P217, from Hadzihasanovic to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade says: "The brigade commander shall use the units at his own discretion." So the 3rd Corps is clarifying who is in command here of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And another detail: On the 4th of November, Mr. Musija has testified about a Motorola, GP-300. This was linking him to subordinate battalion commanders in Vares, operating in the town. And this is indirectly confirmed also by Podzic, who is in the northern part of the town and has testified to Your Honours. He testified when asked: "Who issued you an order?" "I received an order from the commander of the brigade, Mr. Kubura; it was in a written form and it was forwarded to other officers in both oral and written form." So even written orders did go through Vares on that day. Not only the Motorola, written orders. What are the measures taken in the Vares operation? The looting and the destruction by the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and other units was very intense. Your Honours have heard testimony about that. And it was notorious. All superiors of Kubura and other senior commanders involved ordered it to be stopped. And Your Honours find a wealth of orders trying to impose quickly measures from the Supreme Command, P793, P675, paragraph 3; from the 6th Corps, P675, P676; from the OG Istok, P445, P676, P793, P675, P468, P675, P468; from the 3rd Corps, an inference drawn from P446. So basically all superiors were involved in imposing measures. There are indications that even the 3rd Corps had given an order to the 7th to engage the military police. On the 4th of November at 1525 hours, so in the afternoon, it is mentioned here, sent to OG East, "We issued orders to brigades to engage all available military police members in preventing chaos." So the 3rd Corps indicates to OG East "we issued orders to brigades." Who are the brigades? The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade is in Vares at the time. What is the response from the 7th on that day? DK50 tells Your Honours, "We retreated." But where is the engagement of the military police? Your Honours have just heard the 3rd Corps claims "we asked the brigades to engage their military police." Where are the preventive measures against looting and destruction in town? Not at the outskirts. There is another order here from the 5 of November, and Your Honours can see there are four different measures ordered to be implemented. And Your Honours can also see it is delivered to the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. It is requested to impose four measures. What is the response from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade? And, Your Honours, I especially point out the fourth measure. It says: "Vehicles in which fighters are found contrary to this order shall be taken." First the first three orders, and then the fourth on dealing with the vehicles. What is the response from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade? Your Honours see there is three measures, the first three more or less verbatim, implemented as the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was asked. But where is the order that the vehicles have to be seized? This is P478, for the record, here. Where is the order that the vehicles have to be seized? Order 1, 2, and 3 is there, but -- it's implemented, but implementation of the fourth one is missing. So Your Honours see how the implementation on the side of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade is taking place. Yes, we are implementing, but we are not fully implementing. Finally, I want to talk briefly about the checkpoint. Your Honours have heard several times and several witnesses talking about the notorious checkpoint in the south of Vares. No Prosecution witness, however, has been ever asked about this; or in other words, this checkpoint -- I don't want to say "appeared" during the Defence case, but there weren't any questions asked to the Prosecution witnesses whether there is such a checkpoint, and especially whether such a checkpoint was observed by the 7th Muslim -- was operated by the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in the south of Vares. And there were international witnesses, I believe Weckesser, the Prosecution isn't fully certain about this, Garrod. There were witnesses who travelled that day southbound, leaving Vares. So they testified -- they testified -- actually it is -- I see here on the screen it is Weckesser and Hendricsson -- they testified they travelled to or left unhindered in Vares at least until noon on the 4th of November -- 4 of November. So where's the checkpoint, Your Honours? And another detail: Who's the operating authority of this checkpoint? Witness Podzic has testified to Your Honours: "Behind my unit" - and I quote - "behind my unit, at the very entrance to the city, a checkpoint had already been in the process of being set up by the civilian police." The same witness later on specifies what he means: "Right on the heels of my unit" -- on the heels. I think the transcript is not correct here. "On the heels of my unit, there was the civil police, and they set up a checkpoint while I was talking to the UNPROFOR officer." So again the civil police was setting up the checkpoint, coming after the spearheading 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade units. Witness Junuzevic has testified also: "I was in Pajtov Han and MUP was in charge of the checkpoint there." Another indication, you have the civilian authorities operating a checkpoint. Two indications for this. What is the conclusion? At least the checkpoint was set up and operated to a certain point in time by the MUP, SJB. So a checkpoint was already existing as the Defence -- a checkpoint was already existing, if Your Honours believe that this checkpoint was -- operated. However, what is the duty of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade if another civilian authority is already operating a checkpoint and your soldiers are in town causing troubles? It is insufficient - that's the Prosecution's submission - that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade military police simply joined in an already existing measure of other law enforcement agencies. Your Honours, there is obviously already a measure established, so you have forces available -- the military police, it is claimed, who was at that checkpoint, why not sending them into town? Trying to sort out the order or the missing order there. P675 orders Kubura to cease all acts in the town of Vares, not at the outskirts or even south of the outskirts only. So with the military police of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade stationed only outside, a legal vacuum was left in Vares proper. You cannot send your soldiers in town and leave them for what they want to do there and then stand at the outskirts with a couple of policemen and say, "Now you -- you give away all the bags you have collected," and so on and so forth. You must solve the problem on the spot, especially there was Motorola and other ordering facilities for the accused Kubura. So -- and the important point is there were repeated and specific orders from all corps involved in the operation to do something about it. Your Honours have heard about the measures, court measures, testimony from Mr. Ahmetovic, who confirmed that Vares was, so to speak, in the territorial jurisdiction of the Zenica District Military Court. So what are the measures? And this is Hasanagic who's asked: "Were you aware, sir -- or did you in any way come across any documents or information concerning any member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade who was investigated, charged, disciplined, or in any other way prosecuted with respect to alleged crimes that occurred in Vares in November 1993?" The answer: "No. Not a single document of that nature ever reached me, and I have no knowledge of any proceedings having been brought against anyone with regard to Vares." Needless to mention that there is an order in evidence that the fighters of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade who had participated in Vares could go on leave after the Vares operation was over. Your Honours, this concludes the presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's half past 10.00 now. We will have our break, and we will resume at 11.00. According to my calculations, the Prosecution has another one hour and ten minutes available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume, and the Prosecution may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will be concluding the Prosecution's closing submissions this morning. I anticipate taking about one hour, perhaps a few minutes more, but certainly will be within the time allotted to us. I'm going to address you briefly on the issue of the Zenica Music School and repressive measures, and perhaps just a few comments about the -- the counts relating to the Bila Valley. Then I'll discuss in more detail the repressive measures in general, failure-to-punish aspect of the case, discuss with you a little bit about sentencing, and then finally conclude. Let's focus, if I might, Your Honours, on the failure-to-punish aspect of the music school. I'm not going to go into the actual crimes that were committed there. Let me start, however, by reminding Your Honours of a -- of a simple quote from the witness Hasanagic, who was the assistant commander for legal affairs in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And he was, as you will recall, present when that position, that is, the assistant commander for legal affairs position, was formed. We asked him, Your Honours, about any awareness he had with respect to any 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade member being investigated, charged, disciplined, or in any other way prosecuted for alleged crimes committed in the Zenica Music School in 1993, and Mr. Hasanagic replied that he had received no such information and no such information was ever available to him. We'll be talking a little bit more this morning about Mr. Hasanagic and his precise role within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, but at the outset I wanted to, again, draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that the assistant commander for legal affairs within the 7th was unaware of any reports concerning any members of that brigade being disciplined or charged in any way with respect to the music school. Now, Your Honours will certainly recall we've had a wealth of evidence about the relatively notorious nature of the -- the crimes committed in the Zenica Music School and what was happening there. Judge Adamovic, who as you will recall, is a judge of the district military court or was a judge of the district military court in Zenica at the relative time, has testified about how he heard such information and how he would refer persons who brought that type of information to him to the district military prosecutor's office for further action. And again at page 9480 of the transcript, he -- he testified: "We would refer them to the military prosecutor's office to start formal proceedings. It was not just on one occasion." Now, at paragraph 953 of the final trial brief for the accused Hadzihasanovic, the following quotation is -- is stated: "If, as Adamovic told, the whole city was rife with rumours about the music school, the music school being a detention camp, it sounds surprising hearing from a judge who received complaints from civilians about the music school that he actual did not do anything to process the cases, if any." The Prosecution, Your Honours, would submit that this quotation is misplaced, particularly because, as we've just re-examined, Judge Adamovic did indicate what steps he personally took, in terms of informing the district military prosecutor's office, but also he went a step further than that. As reflected on page 9481 of the transcript,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ADAMOVIC SAID
utterances.text: "An investigating judge has jurisdiction that has been instituted by the prosecutor. If there is no such case, then an investigating judge does not have any jurisdiction. Only the prosecutor of the district military court can commence that process." Judge Ahmetovic, who is an investigative judge of the Zenica district military court during the latter part of 1993, also testified that he did not receive any complaints or criminal records or request to open any investigations with respect to the Zenica Music School. That testimony is reflected on page 16218 of the transcript. And again, I take you back to paragraph 957 of the Hadzihasanovic final trial brief, where it is written: "If the whole city was rife with rumours about the music school, the music school being a detention camp, it also sounds surprising hearing from the head of the civilian police who represented the law and public order in Zenica that he did not do anything." Now, Your Honours, we would again submit that to a certain extent that argument must also fail for the simple reason that Mr. Dzaferovic, who was the president of the executive committee in Zenica at the relevant time period testified at page 14227 that "The responsibility of the local government was to provide the ABiH with the material and technical assistance and help with mobilising people." And in response to a question from Judge Swart, Mr. Dzaferovic testified that "The building was mobilised for the Secretariat for Defence for Zenica municipality in accordance with the law," and he also went on, when asked if the visit -- if any visitors would need permission, who -- to whom they would address that request to enter the music school, and Mr. Dzaferovic testified at 14270 of the transcript, that "This would have been done through the 3rd Corps. If a visit was involved, I couldn't directly participate in this. The division of responsibilities was respected during that period." And we would submit, Your Honours, that it's clear that at the relevant time period the Zenica Music School was under the control of the ABiH 3rd Corps and in particular the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. We'll be addressing in a little bit more detail within the next hour repressive measures in general, but our position is that -- that the music school was under the control of the army, of the 3rd Corps of the army, and more particularly the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and its military police unit. Let me just spend two minutes on the -- counts 5 and 6, with respect to the crimes committed in the Bila Valley or allegedly committed in the Bila Valley region. We have fully briefed this -- these crimes in our full -- final trial brief. What I want to ask or focus your attention on very briefly is the testimony of Mr. Izmirlic. As you will recall, Mr. Izmirlic produced a number of computer-generated maps. He explained how those maps were created and produced, and then testified that it was not possible for some of the Prosecution witnesses to see what they claimed to have observed during the relevant time period on or about the 8th of June, 1993. We would simply make two observations with respect to Mr. Izmirlic's testimony: First of all, the witnesses and the locals who were from the places about which he testified had a thorough understanding of and knowledge of the spatial relationships that were involved; they were knowledgeable about the locations of their own homes and the homes of their friends, neighbours, and relatives, so that when a witness said, "I was on a certain location and I saw a certain specific house being burned, we would submit," Your Honours, that that evidence should be given great weight simply because the local witnesses know the terrain. Our second observation with respect to Mr. Izmirlic and his testimony was that the Trial Chamber visited many of these locations, and you yourselves were able to either see or not see from the locations where the witnesses -- or the approximate locations where the witnesses testified that they observed certain things. So our position on that would be the testimony of the local witnesses should be given great weight and also the fact that Your Honours had the opportunity to visit many of these locations and actually see for yourself what was visible and what was not visible. And that's -- those are our only comments here today about the -- counts 5 and 6 as alleged in the indictment. I'm now going to turn to the issue of repressive measures in general, the aspect of failure to punish. We'll start from a very broad proposition, as reflected in two documents, P771 and P773. These are the letters, Your Honours will recall, coming from the Zenica cantonal court and the Travnik cantonal court with respect to the prosecution of ABiH members for war crimes. And I stress that, for war crimes during the relevant time period. Now, we've heard evidence, Your Honours, that the crimes in question in our indictment would not or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perhaps would not have been classified as war crimes and that could be part of the explanation for why there were no war crimes prosecutions of ABiH members during -- for crimes committed during the relevant time period. We acknowledge that. We simply -- those start from the -- the proposition, as reflected in P771 and P773, that there were no cases involving war crimes prosecutions of ABiH members for crimes committed during the relevant time period and at the relevant locations as reflected in the Zenica and Travnik cantonal district military courts. Let's turn again to the arguments as set forth in the Hadzihasanovic final trial brief. Paragraph 175, citing to DH155.2 or /2, the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic says: "It is quite possible that each of the violations alleged in the indictment was the object of one of the criminal reports filed by the 3rd Corps in view of the nature of the crimes covered by those reports." Footnote 117: "For example, see DH155/2, inter alia, aggravated theft, involuntary manslaughter, murder, violent conduct, unauthorised possession of weapons or explosives, inflicting serious bodily harm, rape, robbery, illegal trade, taking a motor vehicle, grave incidents of robbery, and violence to retain stolen goods, crimes against civilians, double murder, fraud, desecration, false impersonation, violating the integrity of a home, abuse in the course of duty, unlawful appropriation of socially owned property." Now, DH155/2 contains a list - this is the document - at the -- beginning at the bottom of this document is a list of the crimes which the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps reported in the period 14 September 1992 through 1 March 1994. And you will, in fact, in this document see a listing of crimes as reported and the number of cases or the number of reports pursuant to each article of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Criminal Code. Again, this document dated 20 March 1994 to the security sector of the 3rd Corps from the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps on criminal reports filed. Time period covers our indictment period as well as a two -- a three-and-a-half-month period prior to the indictment and a two-month period or three-month period after the indictment. We see that the Military Police Battalion, not any of the lower level units but the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps filed 377 criminal reports. These 377 criminal reports involved 804 identified perpetrators and 20 unidentified perpetrators. Paragraph C indicates a breakdown of who these persons that the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion reported. About 40 per cent of them, 40 per cent of the 824 reported persons who were either identified or unidentified, were members of the BH army. More than half of the people reported during this period were either members of the HVO, civilians, a sole member of the MUP, a -- four soldiers of the so-called Serbian RBH, and as indicated previously, the 20 unidentified perpetrators, known here by the abbreviation "NN." Now, I think this document is particularly instructive for a number of -- for a number of reasons: First of all, Your Honours, when looking at DH155/2 should keep in mind that more than 50 per cent of the reports -- the crimes reported in this document relate to persons who were not members of the ABiH 3rd Corps. Second, it's interesting to note that 274 of the reported cases involved civilians, indicating that the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps could at the very least report crimes allegedly committed by civilians. That's being drawn to the Trial Chamber's attention, of course, because in other places we've heard evidence that the Mujahedin were a civilian law enforcement problem or not part of the army. Well, the Military Police Battalion did, in fact, report crimes allegedly committed by civilians. A member of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps was specifically asked if at any point in time the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion detained any Mujahedin. And Mr. Mujezinovic testified that he was not aware of the Military Police Battalion having detained anyone who called himself a Mujahedin. Now, the other important thing to keep in mind, Your Honours, and we would ask you to take a close look at DH155/2 for the reason that the crimes listed in that document are also quite probative. If you compare the crimes that are set forth in that document and the reports of crimes that are set forth in 155/2, you'll see that a number of those crimes, the majority of those crimes, actually, as reported have nothing whatsoever to do with the crimes in this -- alleged in the indictment in this case. And that actually was -- was acknowledged in part by the Defence in the footnote that we saw a few moments ago, when I read out all of the crimes that were contained in that footnote, including things that clearly aren't charged in our indictment, such as rape. So the -- the reported crimes as reflected in DH155.2 are far more encompassing than what are listed in our indictment, point one; and point two, they reflect reports about 40 per cent of which relate to ABiH members. Let's turn to paragraph 172 of the Hadzihasanovic final trial brief, where the Defence assert "It is not possible to conclude that the special military courts were not used to take preventive or punitive measures against members of the 3rd Corps who had supposedly committed one of the violations alleged in the indictment." Well, is that true? Let's take a look at Prosecution Exhibit P284. This is a document dated 10 August 1993. It's a report of the 3rd Corps command concerning legality in the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if we turn to section 3 of this document, which the 3rd Corps is reporting up the chain of command about legality within the ArBiH, we find that at least as of 10 August 1993 there have been no proceedings for special military courts in the zone of responsibility of this corps. Paragraph 171 of the Hadzihasanovic Defence brief, final trial brief. The evidence also sets out that when an offence was both a criminal act and a disciplinary violation, it could be dealt with as a disciplinary violation. And there's a citation at footnote 106 to P325, and a number of articles contained in that exhibit, and we will take a look at these articles in just a moment. There's certainly nothing particularly contentious about the fact that a crime or a particular offence could be both a criminal act and a disciplinary violation. That -- that is relatively a -- a relatively neutral statement, and we've had evidence to the effect that that is certainly the case. The issue then becomes, when you take a look at P325 -- and P325 actually has two documents or contained two documents. The first one, when you first look at this exhibit, is the decree law on special military courts. That's not what we're focussing on now. But if you go several pages in to P325, you find the Rules of Military Discipline. And let's take a look at some of the articles -- or the articles that the Defence cite to in footnote 106 at paragraph 171 of their Defence brief. Clearly the Rules on Military Discipline are -- or have been promulgated and enacted to ensure discipline within the army. Again, nothing particularly contentious about the general provisions, Article 1 of the Rules on Military Discipline. Article 6 stands for the exact proposition that the Defence have cited to; namely, the accountability of a serviceman for a criminal offence or misdemeanour does not exclude his being held accountable for the same offence as a breach of military discipline too if, according to the rules, that offence also constitutes a breach of military discipline. So what are these breaches of military discipline? Well, Article 7 of the Rules of Military Discipline set forth these breaches, and the Defence have cited to three of them. This would be Article 7, subparagraph 1: "Non-execution of or refusal to execute an order undermining of the authority of a superior and senior officer as well as the unconscientious and negligent performance of duty or obligations in the line of duty." In short, Article 7(1) of the Rules of Military Discipline is an orders violation, failure to follow an order. Now, we've heard evidence, and I addressed you yesterday morning right at the outset in terms of the number of orders that the accused Hadzihasanovic issued to follow the law, so presumably it would follow that if the 3rd Corps commander issues an order to obey the law and a soldier disobeys the law, that soldier is both disobeying the law and failing to follow the order of his commander. So presumably Article 7(1) of these rules would in fact apply. But that begs the question, Your Honours, whether someone who burns down someone's house should be criminally prosecuted for that or should simply be disciplined because they failed to follow the commander's order not to burn down a house. Let's look at Article 7, paragraph 6 of the Rules of Military Discipline: "Failure to take the necessary measures to safeguard the lives and health of people entrusted to him, to secure or maintain in a proper state of repair facilities, objects, and means for the purpose of combat readiness, and to regularly supply the military unit or military establishment." Now, in our respectful submission, in the context of military discipline, the first clause or first phrase of this subsection is talking about the responsibility of officers and non-commissioned officers to take care of the people in their units, not to take unnecessary risks with their people. "Safeguard the lives and health of people entrusted to him." As a general rule, that is military language for "take care of your soldiers." Now, that could also -- that could also apply presumably to persons who were being detained; that is, a commander of a detention facility or the soldiers who are guarding people at detention facilities obviously have people entrusted to them, the people being detained. Again, in our respectful submission, mistreatment of detainees rises far above being a disciplinary matter and is a criminal offence. We would submit Article 7, subparagraph 6 of the Rules of Military Discipline is an inappropriate tool to use to punish people who have allegedly committed offences against civilians or surrendered HVO soldiers in detention. Article 7, subparagraph 7: "Negligence in respect of property entrusted to his care, appropriation of military or other property, or infliction of damage to military or other property." Again, the main thrust of this provision is for the soldier or officer to take care of military property entrusted to his care. It prohibits appropriation of military or other property or infliction of damage. Again, we would submit the types of crimes alleged in our indictment are not simple matters for military disciplinary courts or military -- lower-level military disciplinary action. These are criminal offences. Constitutional law expert Trnka was asked some questions about military disciplinary courts. "If we look at the decree law on service in the armed forces, where you find the provisions whereby a member of the military can be sentenced to up to 60 days in prison, whether by his commander or by a military disciplinary court, and keep in mind that's the maximum punishment at a military disciplinary court, 60 days' confinement, is that what you've just referred to when you speak about the jurisdiction inside the military?" "I think that this concerns the violations of the rules within the army, and that presumably is what we were just talking about, the military disciplinary rules." With regard to criminal offences, says Professor Trnka, "it's the military court that is responsible for such matters." He goes on, and he was asked again: "I would simply like you to confirm whether for each of these violations which are in the rules of the military that a soldier can be punished for up to 60 days in prison or detention, whether by his commanding officer or by the military disciplinary court." Professor Trnka says: "Naturally, it depends on the particular situation, the particular case. If the danger, the threat to the social order is minimal, and if there are mitigating circumstances and the crime is listed in the decree that you are referring to, then yes, naturally this is a situation that could occur. But if the threat posed to the social order was not that insignificant, if there was a significant social threat, then the entire case would have to be referred to the military prosecutor's office, or, rather, to the regional military court to deal with." Our submissions on this point, Your Honours, are clear: The crimes listed in the indictment in this case are a significant social threat to the lives and well-being of the non-Bosniak population in Central Bosnia. For the Defence to argue that disciplinary rules imposing imprisonment of up to 60 days' confinement for the crimes in our indictment is, in our respectful submission, inappropriate. Let me return now to the testimony, as I mentioned earlier this morning I would, of the witness Hasanagic, the legal officer -- assistant commander for legal affairs of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. He was asked a number of questions concerning any measures taken against soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and before I get to those I wanted to briefly review what Mr. Hasanagic told us told us were his duties and obligations. "My other duties included the implementation and application of rules and regulations, especially with regard to criminal proceedings, and the point 16 of the Criminal Code, Penal Code of the former Yugoslavia, which had -- which was still in force on the basis of a decree, and that referred to any crimes against humanity, such as genocide, any crimes committed against civilians or prisoners of war or the sick and wounded. In that part of my job, it was my duty to apply the rules and to thus instruct and set an example for the brigade and the subordinated units in order to make sure that all soldiers were well-acquainted with those rules and that they would indeed apply those rules in the field -- or rather, in the course of armed conflict." He was then asked what relationship, if any, he had as the assistant commander for legal affairs with the 7th with the district military court in Zenica. Again, having many mind what his duties and responsibilities were, he told us that on a couple of occasions he visited the district prosecution offices and the court for some points of interpretation, in order to offer legal assistance when members of the 7th were accused of some misdemeanours. "How many times from the 7th of July" -- which is when he assumed that position -- "until the end of 1993" did he go to the Zenica district military court? "Three or four times, roughly speaking," he said. Did he have any dealings with the military court in Travnik? "No, never," he told us. "Never." I then asked him some follow-up questions about these times when he went to the district military court in Zenica, the three or four occasions. He said: "It was members 7th Muslim Brigade. One report was about theft committed by one of our members, and he was brought to trial and he was sentenced. He actually got a prison sentence," the witness told us. Then there were three more cases, again, internal affairs as they were, offences against officers of the 7th, but for the most part it has nothing to do with any acts aimed at persons of another ethnicity. We're talking about abuse of power or of position. In that respect, I remember there were reports against three of our members." I then asked him about that theft case that he mentioned.
