"Who did this -- who was involved in this? What was that all about?" "Well, the treasure of the brigade broke into the brigade safe. He stole some money." Assistant Commander for Legal Affairs Hasanagic was then asked if he was aware of any cases that were prosecuted before the district military court in Zenica where members of the 7th were prosecuted for crimes committed against civilians or civilian property in 1993. "No, I'm not aware of any such cases of any members having been prosecuted for any such offences." Your Honours, it doesn't get much clearer than that, coming straight out of the mouth of the legal officer of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. The same question: Travnik district military court. Was legal officer Hasanagic aware of any cases prosecuted before the Travnik district military court involving members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade for crimes committed against civilians or civilian property? "Not aware of a single case," he said, "and I never spent any time at the state prosecution office in Travnik in the course of the war." Let me conclude with just a -- a few final comments on repressive measures, failure to punish. Let's go back to Prosecution Exhibit P284, the 3rd Corps report on legality in the Army of the RBiH of the 10th of August, 1993. Paragraph 2, or section 2: "The number and type of disciplinary offences possibly committed criminal offences, and other misdemeanours." This section of the report in effect deals with three types or three categories of wrongs: Disciplinary offences, possibly committed criminal offences, other misdemeanours. And on the 10th of August, 1993, what does the 3rd Corps report up the chain of command concerning legality? Regarding the criminal offences that have been committed, not a single one was committed by any of the members of the 3rd Corps command. Your Honours have heard the evidence - and I'm not going to go through it again - or the steps taken by the Office of the Prosecutor to prove a negative. You've heard Investigator Hackshaw testify about that. It's been raised on a number of occasions. We will point out one final aspect of this component of the case, if you will: By no means - by no means - is the Office of the Prosecutor suggesting that a burden shifts or that any burden shifts with respect to what we are required to prove. However, with respect to the court archives, with respect to the relevant court archives, I remind Your Honours of what Madam Residovic told us more than a year ago when the Defence presented some documents to General Reinhardt and the Presiding Judge asked her where these documents came from, and Madam Residovic replied as follows: "In accordance with the Statute of this Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the agreement on cooperation between the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the International Tribunal, at the very beginning of these proceedings, after our client had his Initial Appearance in the Tribunal, the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic as well as General Kubura's Defence addressed the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the basis of the equality of arms, that we should be allowed access to the archives of the state and other archives." "The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed conclusions instructing the state authorities to provide the investigators of both teams with access to those archives. On the basis of this, the Defence has managed to gain access to the state archives. First the army archives; then the archives of the defence Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the archives of the police, the courts, the prosecutor's offices, and all the documents in the binders given to you which do not come from the Prosecution are as a result of our own investigations during pre-trial proceedings." The parties have been through the archives. The parties have been through the archives. Our final comments to you this morning concern sentencing. We have addressed briefly in our final trial brief the primary factors that we assert should be taken into consideration in sentencing, the gravity of the offence, aggravating factors, and mitigating factors. With respect to gravity of the offence, the Appeals Chamber on a number of occasions has informed that the primary consideration in determining a sentence is the gravity of the crime. "Determining the gravity of the crime requires a consideration of the particular circumstances of the case, as well as the form and degree of the participation of the accused in the crime." We have alleged, and it is our submission that we have proven beyond reasonable doubt, the charges set forth in the indictment. Turning to the crimes that we assert have been committed by the accused Hadzihasanovic, that is, the failure to prevent or punish the crimes listed in the indictment - and we have no disagreement with the Defence that that's what we're talking about here; it is his omission. We are not suggesting that the accused bear criminal responsibility for the underlying crimes but, rather, their omission - it is our position that by failing to prevent or punish these crimes, the accused Hadzihasanovic allowed more than 30 murders to go unsolved, to allow the perpetrators of these murders to escape liability and accountability. He has allowed persons who committed crimes in detention facilities to escape liability and accountability. He has allowed individuals to burn and loot Bosnian Croat homes and to avoid liability and accountability. And with respect to soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, the same can be said of the accused Kubura. It is our submission that these crimes are both grave in and of themselves because of the underlying crimes and the effect that that had on the local population, but in terms of the context here, because the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura allowed the perpetrators to avoid accountability for what they have done. In terms of aggravating factors, the personal circumstances of the accused may be considered aggravating factors. Particularly in this case, the fact that both accused are career military officers. And with respect to the accused Hadzihasanovic, it is, in our respectful submission, particularly aggravating that as a former military police battalion commander in the Yugoslav People's Army he failed to prevent these crimes or to punish the perpetrators. There are no mitigating factors in this case, in our respectful submission. It is the practice of this Tribunal for the Prosecution to offer recommendations in terms of sentencing, and in this case it is our respectful submission that the accused Hadzihasanovic is guilty of the crimes we've alleged in the indictment and that a sentence of 20 years' confinement would be appropriate. With respect to the accused Kubura, it is the Prosecution's respectful submission that a sentence of 10 years' confinement would be appropriate in this case. Mr. President, Your Honours, although of course it goes without saying that there have been a number of -- of persons who have come and gone from the Prosecution case in this team, it has been my honour and privilege to represent the Prosecution in this case. We have no further submissions to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before I present my closing argument, Your Honour, I would like to say two things: We have just heard the -- the arguments of the Prosecutor and we will speak for the next six hours. But before I start presenting the final argument of the Defence, I would like to say that it will go down in the history of this Tribunal that in this case, in the case against Hadzihasanovic, the Prosecutor has not found certain mitigating circumstances. Another thing that I have never experienced before is the fact that in his final argument, the Prosecutor has not allowed any room to the Trial Chamber to do their job. If they establish that my client -- that the Prosecutor has managed to prove beyond reasonable doubt to sentence him or, alternatively, if the Prosecutor has failed to do that, to acquit the accused. These are the first things that I wanted to share with the Trial Chamber after we have carefully listened to the Prosecutor's argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to move on to the final arguments of the Defence. Our final arguments over the next six hours will be presented by the counsel and the co-counsel of the accused General Hadzihasanovic. Today, Your Honour, we will be talking about the introductory remarks, about the theory of the defence from the very outset of the proceedings, about the credibility of the witnesses that have spoken about the facts before this Trial Chamber, about the probative value of the elements and the evidence that was presented before you, about the probative value of the testimonies of the -- of the expert witnesses. As for the first three things that I have just mentioned, I will be presenting that to the Trial Chamber myself; whereas, the probative value of the evidence and the expert witnesses will be taken by my colleague, Mr. Stephane Bourgon. Tomorrow the Defence will concentrate on the issues of the Mujahedin, the proof with regard to certain counts of the indictment, and the issue of the measures that our client, General Hadzihasanovic, has taken. Mr. President, Your Honours, our final verbal arguments will be presented in the way that I have just explained. Throughout our presentation of our arguments, the Defence will rely on the arguments that have been presented so far and that you can find in our pre-trial brief, in our opening statement, and in the final written arguments and submissions. Over the next six hours, we will try to use our time rationally and we'll try not to repeat the same arguments again. Your Honour, we are at the end of the trial against a commander of the BiH army, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, at the end of a trial during which both the Prosecution and Defence have presented a lot of evidence. They have called a number of factual and expert witnesses. At the very beginning, I would like to point out that it is the Defence's position that the Prosecution has not managed to prove his case against General Hadzihasanovic beyond reasonable doubt. It is up to you, Your Honours, to make a decision and say whether the accused is guilty or innocent. The right to the presumption of innocence has been provided for by Article 21(3) of the Statute, and it clearly shows who is it who bears the burden of proof. Although in his final argument the Prosecutor has mentioned this issue, we have all witnessed the fact that in this proceeding we have been the ones that had to prove innocence. In every trial, the burden of proof lies with the Prosecutor. In order for somebody to be pronounced guilty, his guilt has to be proven beyond reasonable doubt for every count of the indictment, for every important element of the criminal responsibility. As we all know, this is a generally adopted legal standard. In the sentence in the Celebici case, the Trial Chamber concluded "It is the general principle that the Prosecutor has to prove their allegations beyond any reasonable doubt." This principle is something that has been adopted in the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as in other European states, and it has been expressed in the principle in dubio pro reo, which means whenever there is a doubt, a decision has to be made in favour of the accused. The Defence has presented their views with this regard, and we believe that the Trial Chamber, after a thorough analysis of all the evidence on their own and in their relationship will come to the same conclusion, and that is that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt any of the counts of the indictment. The Defence has received the final brief of the Prosecutor and it has listened to their argument. Without going into the -- the detailed considerations and review of this final brief, because we are going to do that subsequently, I would like to point out the following: It is clear that the Prosecution has chosen a selective approach to the presentation of evidence in this case. The Prosecutor has completely ignored and continues to ignore the Defence -- the evidence of the Defence, although all this time the Prosecutor has claimed that it is their goal to establish the truth. A number of the Prosecutor's witnesses has not been used and it hasn't been explained why some of the testimonies have not been accepted. In the final brief, certain positions and theories of the Prosecution are presented on some of the basic issues that have not been based on facts. Instead of arguments and facts, their approach to evidence has been sensationalist on a number of occasions. The chosen approach of the total accusation has been caused by the desire to arrive at the sentence of guilty even without achieving the standard of the proof beyond reasonable doubt. This approach and method has been further emphasised in the Prosecutor's opening statement. Mr. President, we are here to try a commander. We are not here to try the perpetrators of crimes in Central Bosnia. And as was said in the Prosecutor's opening statement on the 2nd of December, 2003, this is the first clear case of command responsibility in the history of this Tribunal. This is the first trial to -- military commanders for criminal responsibility based on nothing else but the behaviour of their subordinates. Throughout all this trial, the Defence has emphasised that one cannot forget that the object of this trial was the exercise of command responsibility. General Hadzihasanovic is here because he was the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BiH army. General Hadzihasanovic has not been charged with committing crimes himself, for ordering, aiding, or abetting, or in any other way contributing to the commission of any crimes. These acts are provided for by Article 7(1) of the -- of the Statute of this Tribunal. General Hadzihasanovic is here, Your Honours, because the Prosecutor claims that he failed to perform duties that he has as a military -- that he had as a military commander. However, throughout the entire trial, the Prosecutor focussed on the nature and commission of concrete crimes. It is certain that the existence of crimes is of some importance because their existence is an assumption of anybody's responsibility, including the command responsibility. The Prosecutor focussed on -- on crimes, but he failed to establish a link between those crimes and their perpetrators, on the one hand, and the accused General Hadzihasanovic, on the other hand. Although the essence of this proceeding is trial responsibility, the Prosecutor did not offer the structure of the command or the structure of the corps through which the commander exercised his command responsibility. What is even more striking is the fact that the Prosecution has not offered any evidence about the behaviour and actions of General Hadzihasanovic or any other way in which he performed his duties of -- as a commander. Today, after their respective cases are over, and we now analyse arguments of the Prosecution, we can not fail to remark that the general - that the Prosecution wants to convince the Trial Chamber - is responsible for all the crimes that were committed in Central Bosnia because he was respectable, because he was influential, because he cooperated with various bodies, because he was the commander of the 3rd Corps. The Prosecution is pushing back the standard of objective responsibility into the criminal practice, and this standard was long ago abandoned in the jurisdiction across the world. From the very beginning of this trial, the Prosecution has not been able to prevent a single theory based on which the criminal individual responsibility of General Hadzihasanovic for the crimes mentioned in the indictment can be based. Frequent changes of the position, lack of clarity, and lack of the theory of the Prosecution is most obvious in the treatment of the Mujahedin. To what extent the Prosecution presented and managed to present Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the presence of the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia can be illustrated by just one example: The theory that the Prosecution had after the request of -- for acquittal, according to Rule 98, was that in June 1993 there was a temporary division and confrontation between the Mujahedin and the BiH army. This theory was rejected yesterday. We heard a new theory at the end of this trial on the relationship between the Mujahedin and the army. We are kindly asking the Trial Chamber to compare the evidence and what he -- what the Prosecutor said on the 2nd of December that they would prove. Simply put, the Prosecutor failed to prove what they set out to fail [as interpreted]. On the contrary, the evidence showed that the commander Enver Hadzihasanovic behaved as a reasonable commander that, that he complied with all the obligations that stem from the international and local law. The Prosecutor admitted that they do not have any direct evidence on the responsibility of Commander Hadzihasanovic for the crimes committed in 1993 and that they rely mostly on circumstantial evidence. However, the Prosecutor had access to all the archives, the archives of the BiH army, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO, the international organisations, and so on and so forth. Even after six years, after the beginning of the investigation in this trial, the Prosecutor admits that they still don't have any direct evidence. Your Honour, this trial differs from other trials before this Tribunal by the fact that all the archives of the army to which General Hadzihasanovic belonged were opened and accessible to the Prosecutor. Let me just say that as part of the first disclosure, the Prosecutor submitted to the Defence as many as 55.000 documents of the BiH army and after that another several thousand documents. The Prosecutor does not have any direct evidence not because it doesn't have any war documents but for a simple reason: It is these very documents that rule out the responsibility of General Enver Hadzihasanovic. All that the Prosecutor can present to the Trial Chamber is circumstantial evidence. It is not questionable, from the point of view of the Defence, that circumstances can be acceptable evidence; however, when it comes to circumstantial evidence, every established fact has to be taken into account before any inference is made. The main difference between the position of the Prosecution and the position of the Defence with regard to the circumstantial evidence is -- is the following: In order to prove an important element of the Prosecution, the inference has to prove just one fact. The Prosecutor, however, believes that from the totality of the facts one needs to deduct only one doubt and that this proves the whole thing, although other conclusions could be made based on such facts. Such a position of the Prosecution weakens the Prosecution case and makes it unsustainable. With regard to the position of the Prosecution, let me share another comment with you. For the first time yesterday we heard allegations about covering up crimes. Not for a single moment did the Prosecutor present this theory during his case. Is this a new theory that the accused cannot present his case against? As far as we are concerned, Your Honour, this is a totally unacceptable and inappropriate behaviour in any criminal proceeding. As for the theory of the Defence, Your Honours, the theory and the position of the Defence in this case have not changed from the very outset of this trial. And what theory is that? Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked and there was an armed conflict going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This conflict also existed in Central Bosnia during the period of time mentioned in the indictment. General Hadzihasanovic arrived in Central Bosnia with an entirely different task and an entirely different mission; however, the combat and real circumstances imposed themselves on him and he was forced to start establishing the 3rd Corps under very difficult circumstances. Colonel Schellschmidt described very clearly the position that General Hadzihasanovic found himself in. And I quote, page 7920 of the transcript: Question: "With regard to your explanation, you also said that it is very difficult to establish a corps. And if I interpret your words well, you said that having been issued with an order to establish a corps, if you start from scratch, it takes seven years. And if there are already brigades, then it takes three years to establish a corps. My question to you was: What was the position of Enver Hadzihasanovic? Could you please remember what you -- your answer to my question was." The witness's answer to that was: "Yes. I believe that I used an American phrase, 'mission impossible.'" In spite of that, the theory and the position of the Defence is that Commander Hadzihasanovic managed to establish an army corps. All this time, throughout performing his duties as the person who had a task to establish a corps, he was facing two enemies -- two enemies. Throughout all this -- these enemies, he made a constant effort to prevent members of his corps from committing crimes and to punish the perpetrators of such crimes. He performed his command duties and responsibilities in keeping with the law, in keeping with the standards and practice, in the most difficult circumstances that a commander can face. From the very beginning, our position was clear: General Hadzihasanovic was a reasonable and responsible commander who cannot be held responsible for any of the crimes alleged in the indictment. Our position is also that when evaluating proof on the reasonable behaviour of a commander, one has to take into account the actual circumstances under which General Hadzihasanovic performed his command responsibilities. And for just a brief moment, Your Honours, I urge you to put yourselves into his shoes. What was the approach of the Defence to presenting their theories and their positions? From the very beginning, the Defence has offered the Trial Chamber all the evidence that proved that General Hadzihasanovic was a reasonable commander who took all the necessary measures. The final arguments of the Prosecutor is burdened with new arguments, new theories, and new allegations. The oral arguments of the Prosecutor are similar to an opening statement presenting the theory that has to be proven in the future, and like that, the Defence does not offer any new theories. We urge you to look at our pre-trial brief, our opening statement, and you will see that the Defence has proven the things that we set out to prove and that we have -- presenting only those pieces of evidence that we promised we would. As for the credibility of the witnesses, I would like to say that this issue is something that the Prosecutor potentiated in their written submission. The Defence believes that the evaluation of the credibility of the witnesses is a very important issue and that the Trial Chamber should evaluate the evidence of both parties in the proceedings and that it has to put the evidence presented by the witnesses in the perspective of their credibility. The Defence does not share the Prosecutor's position with regard to the evaluation of the credibility of the witnesses. When it comes to the local military witnesses, members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other officials, the Defence believes that they are the only persons who can appear as direct witnesses of the events. They are familiar with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its structures, its competencies, its mission, and the conditions under which it operated. They are the ones who prepared, issued, and carried out orders through the chain of command. These witnesses knew the army from the inside. They knew the ground. They knew the relationships, competencies, and the authorities of the bodies that existed at the time. These witnesses were available both to the Prosecutor and to the Defence. The HVO witnesses are witnesses of the enemy army who had the access to the enemy and their positions with regard to the events that took place at the time. They deliberately painted a negative image of the army because of the role that they played at the time, because of the fact that they were often those who caused certain events. The witness who spoke about the destruction of a house and who failed or did not want to talk about the total destruction of villages, such as Bandol and Velika Bukovica, that were within his reach, cannot be considered a credible witness. The witnesses of the HVO who saw something that, according to the witness Izmirlic, was impossible to see can also not be considered credible witnesses. The witnesses who worked for security services that the Prosecutor called as their own witnesses can hardly be called credible witnesses. Most of the HVO witnesses were under the influence of propaganda and false information that the HVO disseminated in the year 1993. The witnesses who increased the damages cannot enjoy full credibility. In the Strugar case and in the sentence in that case, the -- it says: "Just like that, some Croat witnesses, although sometimes inadvertently, seemed to have blown up the damage that was inflicted on that particular day or they did not make any difference between the damage that was inflicted on that day and the damage that was inflicted during the previous shelling or during the earthquake that happened even before that." Some others tried to minimise the presence of the Croatian military force in Dubrovnik. This is paragraph 7 of the first-instance sentence in that case. Your Honour, we have already presented our position towards international witnesses. We would like to add to that that those people who had not been familiar with Bosnia and Herzegovina before they came to Bosnia during the war, their main duty was not to deal with the armies on the ground and to carry out any intelligence. Their main source of information were locals, who themselves were parties to the conflict. The observers, as we have heard from themselves, observed during the day and they didn't know what was happening during the night. Those were mainly professional soldiers who looked at the things in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the perspective of their own experience in their own countries. Very often they did not understand the events and their causes. As they testified themselves before this Trial Chamber, they did not have any access to -- to the internal military documents in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witnesses who could often succumb to the influence of the propaganda that sometimes targeted them as well, those were mostly younger people, and among them, due to the mission that they carried out, there were significance -- significant difference because of the missions that they had. Those are the witnesses that should be trusted when they say that they saw something personally. However, because of the aforementioned limitations, their views and their conclusions have to be evaluated very carefully and put in the perspective of direct evidence in this case. One thing that we cannot accept in this particular case is hearsay evidence. Witnesses who were also victims, with all due respect to their sufferings, very often increased their suffering and their testimonies have to be evaluated carefully and compared with other evidence. For example, they have to be put in perspective of the international witnesses, reports on what they found when inspecting a certain prison, and doctors who examined certain victims, and so on and so forth. On the other hand, the Defence case -- the Defence witnesses have been accused in the written submission of the Prosecution without having been aware of the fact that they were accused. The approach of the Prosecutor towards the Defence witnesses did not follow any objective criteria and were designed to discredit them. Those witnesses took the solemn declaration before this Trial Chamber. They never refrained from talking about their duties and about their responsibilities. The Prosecution cross-examined them and they were never asked any questions about the truthfulness of their evidence. If such a doubt had ever been present for any of the Defence witnesses, the Prosecutor would certainly not omitted -- would not have failed to ask any questions to that effect. The witnesses have also answered the questions put to them by the -- by the Trial Chamber. None of these witnesses made up facts or covered up any of them. Since most of them were locals, they have to be fully believed and trusted. Allow me, Your Honours, to say something briefly about the way the Prosecutor presented their case. In order to justify their theory, in the presentation of their case the Prosecutor often used partial documents, things taken out of the context, and thus created an impression of the existence of some things that in reality does -- do not exist. In the legal culture of our country in which I gained most of my experience, we rely on some principles that were known already in the Roman law. One of these principles is as follows: Quod ab initio vitiosum est non potest tractu tempore convalescore. What is invalid at the beginning cannot become valid with the passage of time. For example, the Prosecutor -- in translation, this Latin sentence means "what was not valid at the beginning cannot become valid with the passage of time." The Prosecutor tries to put the Mujahedin under the effective control of the army, and he starts doing that by interpreting the interview that Andrew Hogg conducted with Abdel Aziz, although neither the interview nor the testimony of this witness proves that the aforementioned Arabs -- Arabs were ever under the influence of the BiH army or the Territorial Defence as the legitimate armed force at the time. Before I continue, Your Honours, I'm going to use a certain number of documents in order to present my position with regard -- with regard to the way the Prosecution case was presented. I'm going to give you a very thin file containing the documents that the Prosecutor mentioned yesterday, and I'm also going to show -- give you a few maps that I have shown to the Prosecution during the break. I'm not going to use them, but they will merely serve to illustrate the things that I'm going to be talking about. I have these files for the members of the Bench and for our learned friends from the Prosecution. Under tab 1 of this file, you will find the transcript of the interview between Andrew Hogg and Abdel Aziz. The Prosecutor pointed to the fact that this interview is proof that in the summer of 1992 Arabs from various countries arrived in Bosnia and they placed themselves under the control of the army. If we look carefully at the document which was filed long ago, we will see, Your Honours, that in this interview the Army of Bosnia is not mentioned anywhere. The Territorial Defence is not mentioned anywhere, and it was the legitimate armed force in the summer of 1992. Muslims are mentioned in this document, one of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you have heard a number of witnesses that have spoken about the attitudes of the foreigners that arrived in the territory of Central Bosnia and that tried in various ways to get close to the local population. In this document, there is no single reference to the fact that these Arabs were under the leadership of either the Territorial Defence or the army. The question was put whether they were received well by the local authorities, and Abdel Aziz said, "We were well received by the Muslims." Again, the people. The only thing that the Prosecution used to establish a link between the Arabs and the then-legitimate forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the reference made by Abdel Aziz when he said that he was under the control of the Muslim forces. And as for the Muslim forces, Your Honours, on several occasions we've heard testimonies of a number of witnesses who testified before this Trial Chamber. In order to confirm his allegation that the Muslim forces were part of the Territorial Defence, the Prosecutor in paragraph 77 of his written brief calls upon the testimony of Semir Terzic. Without talking about the truthfulness of other facts that this witness spoke about, I would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that this witness said that "The Muslim forces were established on the 10th of May, 1992 and that all the -- that just like all the other units, they were part of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Travnik." As for the footage where he himself could be seen, the witness said it was nothing else but a pledge of loyalty being taken by the members of the Territorial Defence. This was a common practice, according to him, at that time. The -- there is no probative to the testimony of this witness, and this is confirmed by DH1663, that you will find under tab 16 of this file. This is an overview of the staffs and units of the TO Travnik that were under the command of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Travnik on the day of 20 May 1993. In this overview, there is no unit called "Muslim forces." We have heard all the commanders and chiefs of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Travnik that occupied that post in 1992 and 1993. Let me remind you who they were: Zijad Caber, Haso Ribo, Hamed Masanovic, Ahmed Kulenovic, Remzija Siljak, and they were all in agreement when they testified that the Muslim forces were not under the command of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence. The Prosecutor relies on the testimony that the footage was the footage of a pledge of loyalty being taken by a unit of the Territorial Defence of Travnik. If that was the case, then this footage would have depicted at least one representative of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence, at least one of the aforementioned persons who at the time held responsible positions in the Territorial Defence Staff. As we could hear on a number of occasions and see on a number of occasions, none of the persons that I mentioned before could be seen on this footage. From the transcript that the Prosecutor offers as the proof that this was the pledge being taken by the Territorial Defence and the -- and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one can see that this is not the pledge-taking of members of the Territorial Defence and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this pledge is part of the evidence in this case. The witness Terzic recognised on the footage only one person as supposedly the person who was the commander of the logistical base of the 3rd Corps. There's no need for me to -- to offer my position on that. This happened in the summer of 1992, and the corps was established in -- in 1993. Another proof of the Prosecutor in this case is the order of General Hadzihasanovic dating back from the spring of 1993 by which he ordered that the logistical bases of the municipalities, that is, the civilian bodies of authority, had to be transformed into the logistical base -- bases of the 3rd Corps. And this is eight months after the event depicted on the footage. One can believe Defence witnesses, including Ribo Haso, who at the time was the commander of the Municipal Staff of TO Travnik. This is proven by the official record, number P701 that, you can see under -- under tab 2. This note shows that this witness, the commander of the staff of Travnik RH, which stands for Ribo Haso, he complained about the establishment of the units of the Muslim forces, whose leader was Hodza Muftija [phoen], and who recruited people from the regular units of the armed forces. The Prosecutor had an occasion to put these questions and all the others to Ribo Haso, who testified here, but he failed to do it. And the witness Ribo Haso was very clear when he said that in 1992 the Muslim forces were not on the strength of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence. On page 19 of the transcript of yesterday, the Prosecutor mentions the witness Ibrakovic and he mentions the fact that the Arab Sahar was killed near Visoko in -- in the summer of 1992. From this, he infers then in 1992 the Arabs were fighting in the area of the 3rd Corps, which was previously the area of the Territorial Defence, although it is very clear from all the evidence that at the time the territory of Visoko was not part of the territory of the 3rd Corps but, rather, of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Furthermore, the Prosecutor mentions the correction that he suggested to the journalist Hogg, and there is a word in the interview that the witness could not recognise. The word started with the letter "K," and the Prosecutor said that this could be Karaula, relying on the words of the witness Cuskic. During the time of the interview in the summer of 1992, Karaula was not the line of defence, as the Prosecutor claimed yesterday during his final argument. According to all the witnesses, and especially General Cuskic that the Prosecutor relies upon, it was only after the fall of Jajce, that is, in the fall or, rather, the end of October 1992 that the line of defence was established Karaula, which before that was deep in the rear. In other words, direct evidence from the year 1992 clearly shows that the Muslim forces that Abdel Aziz refers to in the interview were not a part of the Territorial Defence or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me illustrate with a few more examples the way the Prosecutor presents his evidence. When he tried to prove that the commander knew about Orasac, which was the place that was later on transformed into a Mujahedin camp, the Prosecutor calls upon evidence number P500 and P501. This is clear in the written submission and in the final argument. The aforementioned pieces of evidence have nothing whatsoever to do with the Orasac that you, Your Honours, visited and that are mentioned in the -- in the pieces of evidence. Already on the example of Zagradje that the Prosecutor wanted to place in the vicinity of Mehurici, although Zagradje was in the vicinity of Kakanj, the Prosecutor had to understand based on the example of Zagradje that in Bosnia several places sometimes bear the same name. From his own evidence -- and now I would like you to look at the evidence after tab 3 and 4 - these are P500 and P501 - one can clearly see that the reference is not made to the Orasac that is a place in the Bila Valley. This place, this Orasac that is mentioned in these pieces of evidence, has nothing whatsoever to do with the indictment. Based on the coordinates in the documents, the Prosecutor could have consulted a map and he could have seen that the place in these documents is between Fojnica and Breza and in other documents he could have seen evidence about the combat activities in the area of the 6th Corps. Why did Prosecutor use the word of only one member of the staff of the Supreme Command in one of his footnotes? Was it to confuse the Defence? And now I would like you to look at the document which is under tab 6, in which you will see that in this part, in the south-western part next to Kakanj, you can find places called Mehurici, Orasac, and Dusina, which have nothing whatsoever with the Dusina, Mehurici, and Orasac which are the object of the indictment. After tab 3, also south of Zenica you will find a number of other places bearing the same or similar names. At tab 8, you will find a place called Orasac, which is south of Novi Travnik. And in 1993, it was probably under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. After tab 9, you will find another place called Orasac, between Visoko and Fojnica. And that is a place referred to in documents P500 and P501. In addition to this very characteristic way in which the Prosecution tries to present non-existent facts, the Prosecution also tried to present the events after the establishment of the El Mujahed by describing the fighting that took place at the beginning of September. That is on page 29 and 30 of the transcript. Although, the Defence -- although the evidence P792 and P740 confirmed the testimonies of Remzija Siljak, Vezir Jusufspahic, and others from the 306th Mountain Brigade, that the El Mujahed was not resubordinated to the 306th Brigade and refuted the allegations of the Prosecution about the way the fighting was conducted during that period of time. The lack of consistency, the lack of truthfulness and sensationalism in the presentation of evidence does not concern only the Mujahedin. The Prosecutor used parts of the evidence of the witness Veseljak Mladen to portray a distorted picture of his testimony. What this witness said about the way the Prosecutor conducted his investigation about the role of the investigative judge, about the role of the military and civilian police, the Trial Chamber will see in the totality of the evidence of this witness and not from the distorted picture of this testimony. We would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the pages 15.991, 15.992, 15.993, 15.994, 16.006 of the transcript, which you can find under tabs 13 and 14. We would like to also point out to the caricature and the testimony about the theft of the cow, although the witness in question explained that those were the measures that were taken in order to protect the civilian population, the Croatian civilian population, and the measures that were put in place in order to deal with the members of the army that might have jeopardised the property and the lives of that population. The Prosecutor treated in the same way the document that was presented to this witness and the document showed that a Croatian, a person acted as an imposter and presented himself as a Mujahedin. The Defence cannot accept that a Prosecutor behaves inappropriately before a Trial Chamber and when he says that Judge Strika is an infamous Judge Strika. The Prosecutor does not know the judge. The judge performed his duties in keeping with the law of his state. And when he refers to this judge in this way, the Prosecutor forgets that in this investigation during 1993 another witness took part. He appeared as the Prosecutor witness; his name is Vlado Adamovic. And this is very clear from Osman Hasanagic's testimony, and this can found in the transcript on pages 12.683. I have tried to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that it is indispensable for every piece of evidence to be looked carefully and to establish its real significance rather than to be misled by the way the evidence was presented by the Prosecutor. This is as much as I have had to say about the three issues that I wanted to raise at the beginning of the final argument of the Defence. And now I would like to give the floor to my colleague, Stephane Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it please the Court. Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Madam Judge. Good day, Your Honours. My purpose is to present to you the Defence's point of view with regard to the probative value that should be attached to the documentary evidence, video evidence, and the testimony of expert witnesses who have been heard in the course of the proceedings. Before I commence with my closing arguments, Mr. President, I would like to go back to an issue raised by my colleague, since I believe the interpretation was not very clear. This has to do with circumstantial evidence, and my colleague said in her own language the following: "When it is a matter of circumstantial evidence, if the Defence proposes a theory that states that General Hadzihasanovic is not criminally responsible," that was the first issue. Secondly, "If this theory is not incompatible with the evidence, in other words, if the theory is a possible one, the conclusion to draw is as follows: Even if there are other possible theories, General Hadzihasanovic should be acquitted." Mr. President, that is the point that my colleague made, and this establishes a link between circumstantial evidence and reasonable doubt, and the Prosecution is trying to minimise this link. I'll now move on to my first subject, documentary evidence. And the first conclusion, the first thing I would like to point out, is that in the course of the proceedings the Prosecution has requested that 959 exhibits be admitted into evidence, and that request has been granted. Out of this total number of documents, about 350 documents were used with the Prosecution witnesses or with Defence witnesses. About 30 per cent -- no more than 30 per cent of the documents used by the Prosecution were verified through witnesses, and this means, Mr. President, that the Prosecution has provided the Trial Chamber a bundle of about 600 documents and they made the following claim: "Your Honours, we are hereby presenting you with 600 documents and it is our submission that all of these documents are relevant. We request that you attach as much weight as possible to these documents, as they reflect the situation such as it was in 1993. We request that you take charge of these documents and that you place them within our immense circumstantial puzzle without asking any questions. All you have to do is trust us and at the end of the trial, we will tell you where all of these pieces fit in the puzzle." The second point I would like to make, Mr. President, is that the Prosecution expects that all the Prosecution -- all the exhibits that have been admitted be regarded as fully valid, as if these documents were completely authentic ones. The Prosecution also adds in paragraphs 5 to 14 of its final trial brief that the testimony that has been heard in the course of the proceedings is not reliable, as it depends on the memory and on the credibility of witnesses; whereas, the documents themselves were drafted in 1993, at the time of the events concerned. In this respect, Mr. President, one may rightly wonder what we have been doing in this courtroom for over 18 months now, given such an approach. It is our opinion that it would have been better for the Prosecution to file the 959 documents and to close its case. At least, this would have allowed us to save taxpayers' money and it would have also allowed us to confirm from the outset that with the exception of a number of documents where the words "MOS" and "Mujahedin" appear, the Prosecution had nothing that they really had to present to the Trial Chamber. And one wonders what the problem is with regard to such an approach. Our answer is quite simple, and this is the third conclusion we would like to draw: A document that has been admitted does not automatically have probative value, and this applies to the documents of the Prosecution as well as to the documents that the Defence presented without doing so through a witness -- through witnesses. The Trial Chamber have mentioned in this decision -- mention this in its decision on the admissibility of Defence documents, and I'll quote: "As a result, the party that wishes to tender a document without doing so through a witness is proceeding in this manner but is taking certain risks. The probative value of the document in question could be diminished as a result." And there is an additional question that arises, Mr. President: Namely, what is the problem with the document that is not being presented through a witness? And it's our submission today that the answer to this question contains several parts. Firstly, "proceeding in this manner" means that the Chamber is deprived of any assistance when it come to interpreting documents, and the Chamber will certainly agree that the documents concerned are a lot more complicated than contracts stating that Peter bought two sacks of potatoes from Paul. The fourth point we would like to make, Mr. President, is that if a document is not presented through a witness and if this document requires an interpretation or an explanation, it is our respectful submission that such a document must be interpreted to the accused's advantage and such a document by itself cannot be used to establish a material fact. The second problem with the Prosecution's approach is as follows: The accused is deprived of his right to cross-examine Prosecution witnesses or the testimony of Prosecution witnesses. And the fifth point, Mr. President, I would like to make is that a document which is not presented through a witness cannot be used to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prove any of the essential elements contained within the charges. The third problem concerning the Prosecution documents is as follows: The lack of weight of a document that hasn't been presented through a witness, even if the Prosecution -- although the Prosecution had the opportunity to use such a document through a witness, that it -- but decided not to do so, not the present such a document through the witness. That is the third problem. And, Mr. President, we submit that when the Prosecution had the opportunity of using a document through a witness and decided not to do so, this document must be set aside. Why? For the following reasons: Because this shows that the Prosecution had -- didn't rely on its own documentary evidence and they didn't believe that the document in question would pass the test of cross-examination. I'll provide you with an example: A document that was apparently shown to an HVO witness, with regard to the Totic kidnapping. There is a small -- a short paragraph in this document which says that the document was provided to the witness by Merdan Merdan [as interpreted], as testified before the Chamber. The Prosecution did not use the document, but the Trial Chamber was more far-sighted than the Prosecution and showed the document to General Merdan, who said, "Well, I'm sorry, but I am not able to recognise this document. I'm not familiar with these contents. I did not provide someone from the HVO with a document concerning Totic." This is an example, and this is the reason for which the Prosecution on a number of occasions decided not to proceed in this manner, and this happened on a number of occasions in the course of the proceedings. Tomorrow I will provide you with a list of documents with regard to this matter. Mr. President, naturally the Prosecution may have decided not to use a document because the Prosecution believed that they should leave it to the Trial Chamber to decide to use a document in its place. This may be part of the Prosecution's strategy and we're not claiming that they don't have the right to adopt such a strategy. They might expect the Prosecution to use a document that they don't want to use because they know that the witness's answer might be different. This is a strategy that one can be adopted, so one strategy among many others. However, if the Trial Chamber does not use this document, the Prosecution must be aware of the fact that they are taking certain risks, that they're proceeding in this manner at their own risk. I'll now deal with attaching probative value to certain documents. We have already informed the Trial Chamber of our position with regard to this subject. We would just like to take advantage of this opportunity to sum up our position with regard to the weight that should be attached to certain documents. I'll deal with various types of documents, and I would first like to deal with official documents very briefly. For example, if we take the case of decree laws. If such laws were in force in 1993 and the document was one known by persons who had to apply the law, it necessarily has much probative value. And this is the reason for which the Defence accepted all the documents -- agreed to all the documents that were such official documents. There are then documents that come from international organisations, from the European Community Monitoring Mission, for example, documents from UNPROFOR, and BritBat documents. And these documents necessarily include milinfosums. For the reasons mentioned by my colleague with regard to international witnesses but also, and above all, given what has been said in this regard by the witnesses Sir Roderick Cordy-Simpson, Colonel Stewart, and a witness whose name I cannot mention and unfortunately I don't have the witness's pseudonym, but it's another witness - I'll find the pseudonym later - this witness, as well as the two other witnesses that I have already mentioned, dealt with the subject of milinfosums. The existence of these documents is not problematic in itself, and as a result the Defence immediately agreed to having all these documents admitted into evidence and we didn't ask any other questions. The problem is the probative value of these documents. And in the best of cases the probative value of these documents is minimum. The witness I was referring to, Mr. President, is Witness HC. There was an observation made by an international witness which is made viva voce or which is contained in a document, naturally has much value for the reasons already mentioned by my colleague: The witness is independent, the witness is on the site, he's a member of the international community, he is objective; he might say, "I saw a man with a beard," and we can't doubt such a statement, but the comments made or the opinions presented or the conclusions drawn from the observation made by an international witness does not have any probative value unless it has been subjected to the test of cross-examination. And that brings us back to the beginning. The following category of documents, Mr. President, contains HVO documents. Given all the evidence that we have heard with regard to HVO propaganda - and HVO has admitted that there was such propaganda, and this is known by international witnesses and local witnesses - but this propaganda machine has been quite clearly recognised in the evidence, and we believe, Mr. President, that the Chamber has to exercise much caution before granting any value to these documents. That's all the more true if the documents in question were established by the HVO propaganda department. The Trial Chamber in the Strugar case emphasised the following with regard to documents. And I quote, paragraph 7 -- I'll quote in paragraph in English. [In English] "More regrettably, the Chamber has also been forced to conclude that some of the oral and documentary evidence is deliberately -- pardon -- deliberately contrived and false." [Interpretation] Mr. President, a document is not automatically true. Finally, there is also the physical appearance of HVO documents that can be revealing. I'm referring to the traditional indicia of reliability, such as a signature, a stamp, a number of copies, a sent or received stamp, or references to other documents. Your Honours, it is our submission that this is applicable even more to documents that are called protests [as interpreted]. I will just use one example. I'll just use one example, P68 -- 694. It was a document used by my colleague with regard to the Sretno Motel. When you have a look at this document, we come to the following conclusions: It's a propaganda document that was prepared by the propaganda department. It was a document described as a protest. But what is more important is that it's a document for which there were four copies, but there were five addressees and one copy remained. Who are the two addressees who did not receive a copy? With such a document, if there is no evidence heard in the course of the proceedings, no weight can be attached to such a document. It's a document that did not have any sent or received stamps on it, a document that was allegedly sent to the joint command of the HVO and the army. It was allegedly used -- it could have been used with many witnesses heard by the Chamber. It's quite obvious, Mr. President, that such a document has to be rejected. The following category of documents I would like to deal with concerns BiH army documents. These documents are interesting, Mr. President, to the extent that they were used with witnesses. If that was not the case, they can be used to establish the existence of certain facts but one cannot use such documents or an interpretation of such a document against an accused unless we have additional elements or additional explications or unless we have a link between such documents and other documents. And yet again we cannot attach weight to such documents if it could have been used with a witness but was not used with a witness. And finally, there are interviews or newspaper articles, and these documents have to be used with much caution, and the reason to exercise caution when using such documents is as follows: The person giving an interview, unless doing so unexpectedly, usually has an objective or a message he wants to convey. I'll just provide you with two examples: P112. It is an interview between Hogg and Mr. Aziz. My colleague dealt with this. Who is Aziz? Did the Prosecution manage to establish his identity and the role he played in 1992? To put the question is to answer it, Mr. President. It's quite clear when one reads through what Mr. Aziz stated that he was functioning in propaganda mode. The Prosecution in its closing argument failed to mention an extract from the interview when he said that there were over 1.000 Mujahedin in Bosnia and that more and more Mujahedin were arriving on a daily basis. This suffices, Mr. President, to state that no probative value can be given to this document. A second example I would like to provide you with is P763. I think it's an internal journal from -- from a brigade in 1995. It's through Mr. Aziz -- it was presented through Mr. Aziz who spoke about events in 1992. Mr. President, we are all familiar with the type of articles that we can final in public organisations. And this is all the case when we deal with internal military journals. We do not doubt that there is some substance in the Hadzic [phoen] article, but what is the true part and which part concerns the history of war, "the history of sin," as General Duncan would surely call it. I'll now move on to my next part of my closing argument. Mr. President, I would now like to deal well video evidence. Before I do so, I would like to briefly address the matter of war journals that were admitted into evidence by the Chamber on the 22nd of June. Mr. President, we were asking ourselves why such a decision was taken at such a stage, but it would not be appropriate for me to linger on this matter at the moment, to dwell on this matter. Unfortunately, we have not had enough time to include the contents of these journals in our closing arguments. On the other hand, the Prosecution, given all its resources, all its personnel, have had all the time they needed to react to the Chamber's order. We'll take advantage of our closing argument to include these journals in our submissions because the journals that we have examined in detail confirm in all respects the context that we wanted to demonstrate to the Chamber in the course of these proceedings, the context that made the task of all the members of the 3rd Corps almost impossible. With regard to these journals, Mr. President, we believe that they fall under the -- in the category of documents that have not been attended through witnesses. As far as video evidence is concerned, I'll be very brief. I'll content myself by emphasising the arguments of the Defence when these documents were admitted. We explained to the Chamber why a video document that was obtained from an unknown source, a video document whose author we did not know, a document that was compiled without knowing how, and given that we didn't know when such a document was made, given that the contents were used for propaganda, the objective of the video was for propaganda, given that the identity of the persons concerned, with a few exceptions, was not known, given that the sites could not be identified with a few exceptions, given all of these reasons, we have explained to the Chamber why we believe that such a document should not be admitted into evidence. The Trial Chamber decided otherwise, and naturally we will respect the Trial Chamber's decision. Nevertheless, it is our submission that this video evidence should not be given any probative value. In addition, Mr. President, in our opinion, given that the Prosecution feels the need in its trial -- feels the need in its trial brief and in its closing argument to use such evidence, shows how weak the Prosecution case is. I'll now move on to the last subject, Mr. President. This has to do with the probative value that should be attached to expert witnesses. I'm referring to expert witnesses who have testified before this Chamber. First of all, there is the expert witness who testified about the history of Bosnia, a Defence witness. And, Mr. President, this witness drafted a report which was admitted into evidence. He then testified and he was cross-examined. The Trial Chamber also had the opportunity of putting questions to this witness. In our opinion, this witness assisted the Chamber in a field that they were not familiar with, and this witness proved, without any doubt, at least the following facts: In the course of history, the territory of Bosnia, with the exception of a brief period, was always recognised within well-established borders. Secondly, the -- Bosnia was always a multi-ethnic, a multicultural, and multi-religious community. Thirdly, the inhabitants of Bosnia, regardless of the ethnic groups they belonged to, always lived in the same areas and had done so for a long time. Fourthly, for this reason, dividing Bosnia along ethnic lines could only be done with ethnic cleansing, the kind of ethnic cleansing carried out by the VRS and the HVO, but the ABiH did not conduct such ethnic cleansing. They just defended their territory. Then there was the expert in constitutional matters, another Defence witness. He also drafted a report which was admitted into evidence. He testified and he was cross-examined. In our opinion, Mr. President, this witness was of much assistance to the Chamber. He assisted the Chamber in a field that the Chamber was not familiar with and he proved the following facts beyond any doubt. And yet again, he proved these facts in addition to many other facts: In 1992 and 1993, the ABiH was subordinated to the state. The ABiH and the 3rd Corps had no authority over civilian bodies. In 1992 and 1993, the institutions in Bosnia functioned but in a reduced capacity and under extremely difficult conditions. The numerous changes made to the constitutional order by the Presidency created the opportunity for civil organs to interfere in military affairs, and there were in fact such cases of interference. They interfered with the civil organs, not with the constitution. The judicial system of Bosnia existed and functioned independently of the ABiH, and this included military and district courts. All joint activity between the army and the civil bodies was based on the principle of cooperation alone. Mr. President, this witness also dealt with discipline within the 3rd Corps as well as with delegate issues, such as granting nationality to members of the army who were not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But no one asked him any questions about this matter. We submit that his -- his report is reliable. The testimony of the judge and Professor Trnka was never put into question by the Prosecution when they cross-examined him. We claim that this witness's report and the testimony of the witness should be given maximum probative value. And finally, Mr. President, I'd like to deal with the military expert called by the Defence, General Karavelic. In one -- in his -- in their brief, the Prosecution asked the Chamber not to give any weight to the witness. The Prosecution mentioned the methodology employed by General Karavelic. Mr. President, it is our submission that the Prosecution made a very grave error in this case. How can the Prosecution have any doubts about the credibility of General Karavelic given that he was a key witness for the Prosecution in the Galic case, who was sentenced to 20 years for the siege of Sarajevo and for the murder of such a large number of people that no comparison can be made with the current case. General Karavelic was also called as a witness for the Prosecution in the Halilovic case. In addition, the Prosecution called General -- mentioned General Karavelic no less than 30 times in its final trial brief. Mr. President, the Prosecution cannot have its pudding and eat it. What's the quality of General Karavelic as an expert? First, there are objective criteria. He held the same position as the accused in this case; he was the commander of an army corps. He was the commander of a corps in the same forces. He was familiar with the objectives of the army. There are subjective criteria. He was a witness and acted in the same war. He had the same experience. He had to desert the JNA in order to join the ABiH. It's an impossible situation. As far as qualifications are concerned, General Karavelic has everything. He was a commander, a member of the staff at all levels. The methodology used by the Defence was as follows: There was a member of a military who came to present an expert military report. The Prosecution says that there's a problem with the testimony that they were provided with in summary form, but the problem is that the Prosecution, if they had a problem with the facts, well, the witness was there in front of them for days; the Prosecution could have cross-examined the witness about the events in question but they did not do so. In its final trial brief, the Prosecution says that Karavelic's report is just a preliminary sketch. In fact, yes, that is the case. That's what we wanted. We put some very precise questions to this expert, and we asked the expert to provide us with precise answers in his military report, and he provided precise answers. In our opinion, Mr. President, this witness's answers are extremely important. The methodology used by the expert should also be emphasised here, analysed; the events at the end of his report and divided them into five categories. He first established the facts and then said why such a situation could have had an influence on a commander at the level of which the accused commanded, at the level of a commander of an army corps. He said what one could expect from a corps commander in such a situation. He also described on the basis of all the evidence that he had seen - and he had seen all the evidence - he also described what the commander did, in his opinion, and then he drew certain conclusions. In our opinion are two possible reasons for the Prosecution to complain: Did he use the right facts, and did he really report on what General Hadzihasanovic had done? But it's not now for the Prosecution to make criticisms. They should have done so when the witness was here. That's when General Karavelic should have been told, "General, I tell you that in paragraph 2B of your report you say that the general took certain measures. Tell me, what kind of measures are in question? Because I do not believe you." But no, they decided not to do anything. But now it's too late. Nothing was done. The Prosecution made its choices. And whether it's an error or not, this is not the accused's problem. Was the Prosecution in agreement with the expert? Did they believe that they could not attack the expert? Did they show weakness? This does not concern the accused. What is important is that the testimony was heard and the testimony provided was extremely relevant. Two examples of questions posed by the Prosecution: In the first case, the Prosecution tried to outline a question to the expert. They tried to make the general say that finally in the end the situation in Bosnia was not a catastrophic one. To use a very -- an expression used in Quebec, "the response was flying in the face of the Prosecution." The witness said that the situation was not only catastrophic but one could compare such a situation with someone who lacked oxygen and was about to drown. The second example: At the beginning of the presentation of their closing argument, the Prosecution quoted a paragraph from the expert report according to which a commander must not allow himself to use resources to deal with a case that seems to be important but will prevent him from accomplishing his mission. If we judge on the basis of what the Prosecution said yesterday, they didn't understand anything. The witness quite clearly explained what he meant. The witness explained, "You can say that General Reinhardt or such-and-such a general said that as far as defending a territory is concerned, as far as the situation in the territory is concerned, well, this does not change the responsibility of the witness. This does not change legal observations." But the -- that's what the expert witness said. He said that "One always has legal obligations. But when there are no legal obligations, one must not allow oneself to use resources that will put other people's life at risk and that will put the survival of the state at risk. And that's the level we are dealing with in the case of General Hadzihasanovic. It was the survival of Bosnia that was at stake. So when the problem of the Mujahedin appeared at the beginning, it was not a legal problem. It was not a legal obligation. As the problem became more serious and as it endangered his mission, he had to dedicate more resources to dealing with this problem. Mr. President, this subject has been dealt with in the questions, in the case of General Reinhardt, Sir Martin Garrod, General Karavelic. They all mentioned the fact that legal obligations don't change; they always remain. On land, at sea, in the air. That is not the issue. The issue is that the context can prevent someone from carrying out his obligations, can make it difficult for someone to carry out his obligations. In the case of General Duncan -- this was not the case for other witnesses, but he was the chief of -- in charge of training the British Army. He refused to answer a question. He said, "We can -- we can't launch an attack without first giving orders. That's incredible." The same general who dismissed his own subordinate in order to put -- himself invaluable for the Chamber. Mr. President, I'm now referring to the witness Cameron Kiggell because I put a question -- or I believe that the Chamber put a question according to which Kiggell said something that eliminated the possibility of subordinating the Mujahedin to the 3rd Corps. General Duncan said, "Yes, but Mr. President, don't forget that this is a very young witness I had to replace for this reason." However, when we have a look at the 92 bis statement of the person who replaced Kiggell, he said, "Kiggell was never replaced from 3rd Corps because of competence problems." General Duncan mentioned this problem. He mentioned this situation to put himself invaluable. This is the type of man, the type of witness, whose attitude was in all respects pro-Prosecution, someone who preferred to speak about sin and a fishing expedition. Mr. President, I would like to add a few things about General Reinhardt but I will stop here and continue tomorrow. As my colleague has already said, we will start with the issue of applicable law and about the responsibility of a commander. We'll deal with the Mujahedin, with events contained in the indictment. We'll also deal with the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic, the measures taken in 1993. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber apologies to the interpreters because they had to work for an additional quarter of an hour, but it was necessary. So we will continue tomorrow. And the Defence team for General Hadzihasanovic will continue with their closing arguments. We will resume at 9.00 in Courtroom III. Thank you.
